items.title: Voltage-Enhanced Photorefractive Hysteresis in Thin-Film Lithium Niobate Photonic-Crystal Cavities
items.summary: We observe voltage-enhanced photorefractive hysteresis in thin-film lithium niobate nanocavities, causing the resonance to appear at different wavelengths during increasing- and decreasing-wavelength laser scans. Their separation grows with bias magnitude and optical power, but depends weakly on scan speed over 1-200 nm/s. A quasi-static surface-trap model links voltage-biased carrier transport to asymmetric trapping, whose space-charge field shifts the resonance through the Pockels effect. The model captures this hysteresis across three cavities through switching between stable steady states. Space-charge feedback opposes further carrier separation, limiting the hysteresis gap. The model informs photorefractive mitigation and resonance control in integrated electro-optic devices.

items.title: The thermodynamic budget of objectivity
items.summary: An event becomes a fact when enough independent records of it exist such that no operation is possible that leaves all observers ignorant of it again. Records are physical, and creating, keeping, and destroying them have thermodynamic costs. We compute these costs exactly in a minimal broadcast model with a driven central qubit writing records into $N$ initially thermal registers, with work sources and baths at temperature $T$. The basic arguments for the operations are outlined here, with full treatment in the text. Creation of one event record at redundancy $R$ and information deficit $δ$ requires work $W \ge R\, k_\mathrm{B}T \ln 2\, (1-δ) H(\varepsilon)$, linear in redundancy at the Landauer coefficient. Recording in a basis misaligned by $θ$ with the einselecting interaction fails at a critical angle, $θ_c = 2\arcsin\sqrt{H_2^{-1}(δ)}$, beyond which objectivity is unreachable at any work, and below $θ_c$ the optimal work is a closed form in the pointer basis that minimizes the work of objectivity. Reducing objectivity is impossible at any work with access to fewer than $R - R_{\min} + 1$ records, while work protects nothing if given access. Inter-record redundancy is extractable free energy and erasing the accessed records yields a net gain of work beyond the first copy. The second law constrains the destruction of the correlation: erasing a fact from a sector an adversary controls dissipates at least the mutual information erased, but a consolidation dissipates nothing. Records in re-thermalizing media are nonequilibrium steady states, and the minimal power to maintain a record at $(R,δ)$ is the known two-state driving bound evaluated at the record-quality boundary.

items.title: Plasma transport by carrier electrons: delocalization length for heat-flux
items.summary: The kinetic understanding of the three magnetized heat-flux components is unified in the linear regime with a full electron-electron collision operator and a converged harmonic expansion of the electron distribution (up to $f_6$). The delocalization length $λ_d=λ_{ei} Z/\sqrt{Z+4.45}$ is an improved heat-flux non-locality metric accounting for the localizing effect of electron-electron collisions on the electron population carrying heat-flux. Magnetization also localizes the carrier electrons; the delocalization Hall parameter $ψ_d=13.4 χZ/(Z+4.45)$ shows that this occurs at a faster rate than magnetization of thermal conductivity ($ψ_κ= 9.94χ(Z+0.17)/(Z+5.88)$). The traditional Knudsen number, which uses the electron-ion mean-free path, does not fairly represent non-locality across ionization and magnetization; $Kn_d = 8.28λ_{d\bot}/L_T$ should instead be used. Righi-Leduc suppression is found to be the square of the perpendicular suppression, with no additional length-scale required. This approach lays the groundwork for consistent treatment of kinetic plasma transport, with subsequent papers addressing the kinetically-modified induction equation.

items.title: Floquet Decomposition: Floquet Multipliers and Time-Periodic Modes from Period-Sampled Snapshot Data
items.summary: Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) fits one constant linear operator to a sequence of snapshots. When the dynamics, or the view of them, vary periodically, as in a parametrically excited flow or a rotating structure seen in a fixed plane, no such operator exists, and stability is decided by the Floquet multipliers, the eigenvalues of the map over one period. In the paper that introduced DMD, Schmid observed that snapshots sampled at the period of an oscillatory flow would identify the Floquet matrix. We develop that observation into a method and analyze it. The Floquet decomposition (FD) applies DMD to fixed-rate data subsampled once per period; the ensemble Floquet decomposition (EFD) stacks the snapshots of each period into one column, giving one set of multipliers and phase-resolved modes. For linear time-periodic systems both are exact: FD when the measurement at one instant determines the state, EFD when the measurements over one period do---so EFD succeeds with partial measurements. EFD and Hankel (delay-embedded) DMD use the same data matrix with different shifts between columns. With $p$ samples per period, Hankel-DMD returns each Floquet mode as a carrier with sidebands, a comb of $p$-th roots of its multiplier, which the period shift collapses onto the multiplier. The methods are verified against known multipliers; outside their hypotheses, on nonlinear or noisy data, the estimated moduli are biased and are not decay rates. Measurements of velocity, scalars, and acoustic pressure in a swirl-stabilized combustor illustrate the choice of period, rank, and data scaling.

items.title: Schrödinger's Legacy: The Wave Function and Quantum Reality
items.summary: The article discusses how Schrödinger arrived at the formulation of wave mechanics and his legacy on the philosophy of quantum mechanics, focusing in particular on the metaphysics of the wave function. Schrödinger's interpretation of the wave function as electron charge density is generally dismissed or presented only as a curious historical example in the literature. On a closer look, however, while this interpretation was eventually abandoned in favor of Born's statistical interpretation, Schrödinger's idea survived in modern realist approaches to the wave function, such as the mass-density approach and the multi-field interpretation. It also proved to be of great utility in modern techniques and approximations in quantum chemistry to compute the shape of atoms and molecules. Overall, Schrödinger's interpretation of the wave function and his realist understanding of quantum mechanics paved the way to modern attempts to define a clear ontology of the microscopic world, a tradition that survived the Copenhagen interpretation of Bohr and Heisenberg and that is still present today.

items.title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect in Searches for New Physics: from Classical Methods to Machine Learning
items.summary: The look-elsewhere effect (LEE) arises when the location of an effect in parameter space is not specified in advance: scanning many locations inflates the significance of the largest excess, and the local $p$-value must be corrected into a global one. A well-established framework, rooted in the work of Davies and operationalised for particle physics by Gross and Vitells, provides this correction for scans over continuous parameters. Some aspects, however, remain unsettled. The definition of "elsewhere" is ambiguous and ranges from a single distribution to an entire experimental programme. Moreover, the analytical shortcuts of the classical framework do not carry over to searches based on machine learning (ML), which are affected by an implicit post-selection bias that depends on the model's resolution and expressiveness. This review covers the LEE in searches for new physics at colliders, from its statistical foundations to these modern challenges. We discuss the corrections for continuous scans and for multiple discrete tests, illustrated with simple numerical examples, and the interaction between ML and the LEE, which we connect to the broader literature on selective inference. We highlight open problems, including the computational cost of empirical calibration for complex models and the development of analytical shortcuts for ML test statistics, and offer recommendations for reporting discovery significance in both classical and ML-based searches in particle physics.

items.title: Transition Path Sampling for Rare Events in Non-Markovian Open Quantum Systems
items.summary: Rare transitions govern the dynamics of many open quantum systems, but their probabilities and rates are difficult to calculate. Transition path sampling (TPS) of quantum systems has so far been limited to Markovian, perturbative descriptions. Here, we formulate TPS for non-Markovian quantum state diffusion, which is exact for Gaussian baths, extending it to non-Markovian and strongly coupled open quantum systems. For normal-to-superradiant tunneling in the unbalanced open Dicke model, we determine probabilities down to $10^{-8}$ and rates beyond the reach of brute force.

items.title: Modeling capacitor voltage in an RC circuit from data: Construction, breakdown, and revision of an empirical model
items.summary: We describe a guided introductory laboratory activity in which students construct empirical models of capacitor voltage in RC circuits from measured input-output data before circuit theory is introduced. Students may use what they know about resistors, Ohm's law, and conservation of charge and energy, but prior knowledge of capacitor behavior is not used as a reason for adopting a model. The circuits use a 1.5-V battery, resistors, and electric double-layer capacitors with nominal capacitances of 4.7 and 10 F. Their slow responses are recorded with handheld voltmeters and smartphone video, and the capacitance values are presented to students with the unit withheld. To compare circuits, students rescale time by the product of the nominal resistance and capacitance, as proposed by the instructor. On this coordinate, plots of the logarithm of the normalized discharging voltage are approximately straight lines through the origin, providing empirical models. For charging, the corresponding logarithmic plots are clearly curved, and the discharging model breaks down. Using the remaining distance from the final value as the dependent variable gives approximately straight logarithmic plots and provides a basis for revising the model. Rewriting the discharging model in equivalent differential and integral forms allows students to compare changes in charge-like and energy-like quantities with the charge transferred through the resistor and the energy dissipated in it. Standard circuit theory, introduced afterward, describes charging and discharging in a common form and gives these quantities their conventional meanings.

items.title: A Reconfigurable Four-State Sensor Based on Orthogonal Thermal and Chemical Stimuli
items.summary: This article presents a novel four-state refractive index (RI) sensor based on distinct phases of palladium (Pd) and vanadium dioxide (VO$_2$), controlled by orthogonal thermal and chemical stimuli. This is a numerical, simulation-only study: all results are obtained from two-dimensional finite-element method (FEM) simulations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported multi-state reconfigurable RI sensor tuned by external control. VO$_2$ serves as a phase change material (PCM) offering two thermally switchable phases with highly contrasting optical properties, while the hydrogen absorption property of Pd provides two additional phases. Combining these, four operational states are realized: (i) $α$-Pd/low-$T$ VO$_2$; (ii) $β$-PdH$_x$/low-$T$ VO$_2$; (iii) $α$-Pd/high-$T$ VO$_2$; and (iv) $β$-PdH$_x$/high-$T$ VO$_2$. Thermal crosstalk between Pd and VO$_2$ is mitigated through tungsten (W) doping of VO$_2$. This work further introduces conditional state sensitivity (CSS), a novel figure of merit quantifying the optical contrast between each state transition. The proposed sensor achieves a peak sensitivity of 2871 nm/RIU for the undoped reference configuration and 2798 nm/RIU for the practical W-doped device, together with a peak CSS of 16,872 nm/RIU, establishing it as a multi-state reconfigurable platform with reduced thermal crosstalk and potential applications in industrial safety monitoring and optical logic gates.

items.title: Interaction-Free Polarimetry
items.summary: The combination of interaction-free measurement and the quantum Zeno effect has been shown to both increase the signal-to-noise ratio of imaging, and reduce the energy absorbed by the imaged object. So far, however, it has not been used for quantitative polarimetry, the reconstruction of a sample's Mueller matrix. In this paper, we extend this to the polarimetry of diattenuating samples. For polarisation components that the sample strongly absorbs, the protocol identifies the sample with far less absorbed energy than a single-pass measurement, a benefit for delicate samples probed with high-frequency radiation. For weakly absorbing components the repeated passes through the sample absorb more, so the benefit is confined to strongly diattenuating features. A Fisher-information analysis shows that, for a sample with a lossless transmitting axis, the protocol locates the absorbing axis with far fewer absorbed photons than single-pass polarimetry, while it measures partial transmittances no more efficiently per absorbed photon, and that the same sorting of lossy components to one output port responds to retardance and depolarisation.

items.title: Rømer all ears: An auditory analog of Ole Rømer's demonstration of the finite speed of light using smartphones as an acoustic vernier
items.summary: We present an undergraduate experiment for teaching Ole Roemer's 1676 method for demonstrating the finite speed of light. Two smartphones emit periodic sound pulses whose synchronization is evaluated directly by the observer's hearing, acting as an "acoustic vernier" that achieves millisecond travel-time resolution without microphones or external sensors. Because the measurement relies strictly on propagation delays between stationary stations, it establishes a direct experimental analogy to Roemer's original argument and dispenses with auxiliary wave phenomena absent from the 1676 analysis, such as acoustic beats or the Doppler effect. The pedagogical strength of the experiment lies precisely in this direct appeal to the senses. Loss of synchronization becomes perceptible starting at a separation of approximately 5 m and grows progressively clearer across several tens of meters. Despite its simplicity, systematic blind measurements determine the speed of sound in air with single-run uncertainties of 2 to 5 m/s (around 1%) and agree within 1.1% with theoretical predictions across ambient temperatures from 9 to 25 $^\circ$C. Beyond numerical measurement, anchoring the method in explicit sensory perception helps to clarify the recurring conceptual entanglement between Roemer's geometric delay and the kinematic Doppler effect, while highlighting how this same travel-time principle underpins contemporary astrophysical techniques, such as pulsar timing and eclipse timing variations (ETV).

items.title: HydróDex: gotta match 'em all!
items.summary: First-order phase transitions can source a stochastic gravitational-wave background within reach of LISA and other future detectors, with sound waves in the plasma typically providing the dominant contribution. Predicting the resulting gravitational-wave signal requires determining the stationary fluid profiles around expanding bubbles. We present a complete hydrodynamic classification of these profiles in the constant-sound-speed model, which generalizes the bag model by allowing the sound speeds in front of and behind the wall, $c_+$ and $c_-$, to differ. Solving the matching conditions at the wall and evolving the surrounding plasma, we recover the known direct and inverse detonations, deflagrations, and hybrids, and uncover mixed hybrids, a new class with rarefaction waves on both sides of the wall and oppositely directed fluid flows. For a sufficiently pronounced hierarchy $c_+>c_-$, multiple stationary profiles can correspond to the same wall velocity $ξ_w$ and asymptotic transition strength $α_N$. This non-uniqueness arises because this parametrization discards thermodynamic information and is resolved once the underlying microphysics is specified. We compute the kinetic-energy budget and acoustic gravitational-wave spectra within the sound-shell model, finding that mixed hybrids introduce no additional spectral feature and can be mimicked by ordinary direct or inverse hybrids with substantially different fluid profiles. Finally, we release HydróDex, a public code implementing the complete classification, profile construction, energy-budget calculation, and gravitational-wave prediction.

items.title: Plasma transport by carrier electrons: Nernst advection beyond the heat-flow analogy due to kinetic stress
items.summary: Nernst advection of magnetic fields down temperature gradients is lowered by kinetic stress from the $\underline{\underline{f}}_2$ electron distribution harmonic, which allows fluxes to stream past one another without isotropizing their lateral momentum. The long-held tie between heat-flow and Nernst advection is disrupted. When the distance between electron collisions is comparable to the magnetic field length-scale $L_B$, the kinetic stress affects magnetic transport in plasmas otherwise regarded as classical. This is from carrier electrons being deflected back and forth over the course of their trajectory. The field structure Knudsen number is defined: $Kn_B=14.8\frac{λ_{ei}}{L_B}\frac{Z+0.40}{Z+4.86}$, with Nernst velocity halved by kinetic effects at $Kn_B=1$. The kinetic stress is relocalized by magnetization, following the relocalization of heat-flux. Righi-Leduc heat-flow is found to be similarly suppressed by kinetic stress. The linear results of this paper are found to faithfully represent the non-linear evolution of magnetic field at a heat-front, indicating that low-$Z$ plasmas throughout magnetized-HED are demagnetized more slowly than previously anticipated.

items.title: Fewer Parameters, Longer Runtimes: The Wall-Clock Cost of Hybrid Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks
items.summary: While hybrid quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks (QCPINNs) are often described as efficient because they have fewer trainable parameters than classical PINNs, parameter count does not measure wall-clock cost. To examine this gap on a one-dimensional seawater temperature diffusion benchmark, with the quantum circuits simulated on a CPU, we time the four cumulative stages a PINN needs (the forward pass, the first- and second-order input gradients, and the PDE-loss parameter gradient) for a classical PINN, four hybrid configurations that differ in qubit count and circuit depth, and size-matched classical controls that share the hybrids' classical layers. We find that the hybrids are 14-56x slower than the classical PINN for the forward pass and 10-97x slower for the PDE-loss parameter gradient, and even against the size-matched controls, they remain 9-85x slower. Further, over the tested ranges, runtime increased approximately exponentially with qubit count, approximately linearly with circuit depth, and sub-linearly with batch size, while for the circuit-only forward pass, a second simulator backend was 10-165x slower under the same calling pattern. Although the hybrids have 38-44% fewer parameters than the classical PINN, this reduction comes from their smaller classical layers, as the quantum circuit accounts for at most 2.5% of each hybrid's parameters. Yet parameter count failed to predict runtime even among the classical networks, since the size-matched controls, despite having fewer parameters than the classical PINN, run slower than it. Our conclusion is that fewer parameters did not mean lower cost: every hybrid took at least ten times longer than the classical PINN at every stage, and the gap grew quickly with the number of qubits.

items.title: A general-purpose electron density model for molecular chemistry
items.summary: Universal machine-learning potentials predict molecular structure and stability at the accuracy of quantum mechanics, for a fraction of the cost. Properties derived instead from knowledge of the electronic structure give profound insights into chemical reactivity, but are not accessible with the same ease or transferability. We train PET-rho-OMol25, a model of the ground-state electron density and spin polarization of molecular systems on four million OMol25 structures in multiple charge and spin states. The model makes predictions for entire proteins in a few seconds on a single GPU, and enables estimation of important diagnostics of molecular structure and reactivity, such as vibrational Stark measurements, halogen $σ$-holes, hydrogen-bond basicities and core-level shifts, as well as spin density for redox chemistry and magnetism. PET-rho-OMol25 has an accuracy close to density-functional theory, with its least reliable predictions flagged by its built-in uncertainty estimator, for most properties and classes of compounds. It can be used as a drop-in replacement for electronic-structure calculations of the density, making insightful analyses available for larger and more complex structures.

items.title: Observation of a Förster Resonance in a Heated Rydberg Atom Ensemble
items.summary: Rydberg atoms in thermal vapour are of increasing relevance for a range of emerging technologies including compact electric field sensors, where state energies are detected via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT). However, at increased atomic number densities, the Rydberg EIT response becomes non-linear, resulting in distortion of the spectral lineshape. It is thought that this non-linearity mainly arises due to ionisation, although accurate quantitative modelling of the spectrum and assessment of other physical processes remains challenging. In this work, we address these issues in a combined theoretical and experimental study, constructing a model that accurately reproduces observed EIT spectral profiles. We show from analysis of lineshape shifts that while ionisation accounts for most of the non-linearity, it is also possible to observe Rydberg interaction effects for strongly-coupled states near a Förster resonance.

items.title: ENSO-linked redistribution of post-monsoon tropical cyclone energy between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal: 1982--2025
items.summary: Tropical cyclones in the North Indian Ocean (NIO) form in two sub-basins, the Arabian Sea (AS) and the Bay of Bengal (BoB), which are usually studied separately, with their relationship to the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) treated as stationary. We develop a joint inter-basin statistical framework and apply it to 416 disturbances from quality-controlled IBTrACS best tracks for 1982--2025, with harmonised IMD and JTWC intensities, ERA5 and ERSSTv5. The framework tests whether ENSO changes the basin total or redistributes energy between the sub-basins, separates its effect on formation from that on intensification, attributes each sub-basin's response to environmental terms along individual tracks, and tests stationarity and the record length needed to detect trends. In October-December, ENSO redistributes rather than changes the total: for a one-standard-deviation increase in Niño-3.4 (about 1 $^\circ$C), accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) is multiplied by 1.89 in the AS and by 0.63 in the BoB, while the NIO total shows no detectable change (factor 0.99 [0.74, 1.32]). ENSO acts on intensification, with no detectable effect on formation: the odds that a cyclonic storm becomes very severe rise about fourfold in the AS and halve in the BoB, through lower vertical wind shear (VWS) over the AS and weaker low-level vorticity over the BoB. The relationship has changed: El Niño lowered total NIO energy in 1982--2003, but in 2004-2025 AS gains balanced BoB losses (change p = 0.016). Very severe storms and rapid intensification increased in the AS only, and no 15-year window detects this increase, so about three decades of data are needed. The post-monsoon IOD signal can hardly be separated from ENSO, and August Niño-3.4 gives modest skill for the AS-BoB partition but none for the basin total.

items.title: A 2D fluid model in BOUT++/Hermes-3 for simulating detached divertor plasmas in tokamaks
items.summary: Detached divertor operation is essential for controlling target heat fluxes in future high-power tokamaks. We present a two-dimensional fluid model implemented in BOUT++/Hermes-3 for simulating detached divertor plasmas with plasma-neutral interactions and fixed-fraction impurity radiation. We report improvements to the PETSc SNES-based steady-state solver used for two-dimensional axisymmetric transport simulations with fluid neutrals and assess the performance of several sparse-solver preconditioning strategies. For the cases considered here, STRUMPACK used as an ILU preconditioner with low-rank compression provides the most favorable performance, reducing the linear-to-nonlinear iteration ratio and achieving approximately a fivefold speedup relative to \HYPRE{}-based configurations. The optimized solver is then applied to DIII-D shot $\#174287$ at 4000~ms to characterize detached divertor conditions. Cross-field transport coefficients are adjusted to reproduce upstream experimental profiles, and detachment is modeled using nitrogen fixed-fraction radiation. Steady-state particle and energy balances are evaluated by decomposing the density and pressure equations into their transport and source terms. In the outer divertor, electron energy losses are dominated by ionization and impurity radiation, while ion energy losses occur mainly through collisional transfer to electrons. An upstream separatrix density scan shows decreasing target electron temperature and a rollover of the integrated target ion saturation current at higher $n_{e,\mathrm{sep}}$ consistent with expected detachment trends. These developments establish a foundation for future multispecies simulations. Hermes-3 is publicly available on GitHub under the GPL-3 open-source license.

items.title: Diagnosing internal leakage currents through magnetometry of lithium-ion cells
items.summary: Internal leakage currents are difficult to detect and to localize through measurements at the terminals of lithium-ion cells. We measured the magnetic fields of pouch cells non-invasively with a magnetometer while a battery cycler set the current and recorded the voltage. A three-axis magnetoresistive sensor remains fixed inside a three-layer magnetic shield, and two linear stages move the cell in two dimensions relative to the sensor to acquire a map of the magnetic field above the cell. The field of an intact cell was linear in current from 10 to 420 mA, and its maps were symmetric between charge and discharge. To create internal leakage currents, two 600 mAh cells were damaged by mechanical indentation. Both cells developed a magnetic field at zero applied current that decayed over hours, while the cell voltage showed a loss of charge by self-discharge. This field breaks the symmetry between the charge and discharge maps, which allows leakage to be detected while the cell is being cycled. At rest, the setup detects leakage currents down to about 1--3 mA. The results highlight opportunities for battery diagnostics and safety, and may help in designing techniques for characterizing soft shorts.

items.title: Automatic dual basis sets for self-consistent field calculations
items.summary: Density functional theory (DFT) has long been the workhorse of electronic structure theory, and it is experiencing a new boom thanks to big data applications and machine learning. A DFT calculation requires the iterative solution of the self-consistent field (SCF) problem, whose cost is the product of (i) the number of SCF steps and (ii) the cost of a single step. The number of SCF steps depends strongly on the initial guess, regardless of the SCF algorithm, and quantitative DFT accuracy is known to require at least a polarized triple-$ζ$ basis set. However, a qualitatively correct solution may often be found already in a smaller \emph{dual basis} (DB), which can then bootstrap a calculation in the full basis set. Traditionally, the DB is chosen by hand for each application to enable robust convergence to the ground state. In this work, we pursue automatic generation of DBs for SCF calculations. Our generator constructs a pruned orbital basis from the target orbital basis for a predefined precision threshold and a given Fock matrix. As expected, the larger the basis set is, the smaller the fraction of kept basis functions. The DBs produced by our algorithm exhibit similar performance for a wide range of systems from the first 4 periods of the periodic table. Ultimately, we find that presently available initial guesses for the Fock matrix are not accurate enough to unlock the use of adaptive basis sets, and believe that the same limitation may hold for similar attempts for basis compactification.

items.title: First Order Real Resonant Digital Filters and A Novel Orthogonal State Generator
items.summary: We describe FOREST, a real, first order digital resonant filter and orthogonal state generator. We show that in spite of the imaginary nature of the roots of the transfer function of a resonator, appropriate interpretation of this transfer function nonetheless leads to a practical first order filter with real coefficients. We use a discrete state space model of FOREST to predict the resonator properties, and implement the filter in digital signal processing slices on a digital signal processing platform. Applications are in real time digital signal processing, engineering fields such as mains electricity monitoring and motor control, any application requiring a phase locked loop, and physics applications utilising high-quality-factor resonators.

items.title: Electrostatic effects on settling cloud droplets: from pair collisions to size distribution evolution
items.summary: We investigate how droplet charge and a uniform vertical electric field influence collisions between cloud droplets settling in still air and how these collisions shape the droplet size distribution. We compute collision efficiencies by analyzing the relative trajectories of pairs of spherical, conducting droplets, accounting for droplet inertia, exact hydrodynamic, electrostatic, and van der Waals forces. The hydrodynamic interactions are based on exact two-body solutions for Stokes flow with interfacial mobility and internal circulation. In the absence of an applied electric field, collisions between like-charged droplets are suppressed, whereas collisions between oppositely-charged droplets are enhanced. A vertical electric field promotes collisions between uncharged droplets through induced polarization and, when sufficiently strong, can overcome the repulsion between like-charged droplets. When the larger droplet has a radius of $10$ or $20μ$m raising the electric field strength from $5\times10^{4}$ to $3\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ can enhance the collision efficiency of uncharged droplet pairs by an order of magnitude. Depending on droplet size and field strength, for oppositely charged pairs, an applied electric field can either enhance or suppress collisions relative to the zero-field case. Using collision kernels computed from droplet pair trajectories, we solve the stochastic collection equation with a flux method on a two-dimensional grid that resolves droplet mass and charge. For an initial mean droplet radius of $10μ$m , by $40$ min in every electrified case the large-droplet mode of the mass spectrum reaches a larger radius than in the hydrodynamic reference case. This suggests that electrostatic interactions can hasten warm rain initiation by accelerating droplet growth through collision and coalescence.

items.title: A van der Waals photon-ratchet for enhancing spin defect emission and quantum sensing
items.summary: Spin defects in two-dimensional materials are promising platforms for quantum information technologies and nanoscale sensing. The negatively charged boron vacancy (VB-) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is particularly attractive due to its sensitivity to temperature, magnetic fields, and pressure, but its application is limited by intrinsically weak photoluminescence (PL). Here we demonstrate a van der Waals heterostructure that enhances the PL intensity of VB- by up to 45x at 4 Kelvin while preserving compatibility with ultrathin optoelectronic platforms. A type-I band alignment at the PbI2-hBN interface facilitates efficient interlayer coupling to the defect, and strong spectral overlap supports fluorescence resonance energy transfer. Ab initio calculations indicate that this coupling enables a photon-ratcheting mechanism, in which optical absorption in PbI2 generates a nonlinear polarization that drives VB- excitation. This process is consistent with interlayer energy transfer while maintaining minimal electronic and spin hybridization and preserving optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) contrast. The heterostructure further exhibits improved sensitivity to external magnetic fields. These results establish a route for the enhancement of defect emission via interlayer optical coupling and introduce a general materials strategy for amplifying weak quantum defect signals in nanomaterials.

items.title: The Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model: A Semi-mechanistic Generative Model for Temporal Hypergraphs
items.summary: Many complex networks involve time-varying relations between more than two nodes. Such networks are naturally modeled by temporal hypergraphs. We propose the Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model (HHCM), a semi-mechanistic model for temporal hypergraphs that combines a Hawkes process to model the timestamps of hyperedges with a noisy copy mechanism to model the nodes present in hyperedges. Each hyperedge is either generated as an exogenous event with a baseline rate or an endogenous event as a noisy copy of a previous hyperedge. Our proposed model can be used for credit attribution, where the objective is to quantify the influence or contribution of a prior hyperedge to a current one. We apply the HHCM to perform attribution on several real network datasets with higher-order relations, including email networks and militarized interstate dispute networks.

items.title: Morphogenic necking of surfaces
items.summary: Surface morphogenesis occurs across biological scales, from subcellular vesicles and cells to visceral organs, tissue organoids, and whole organisms. Since morphogenesis often involves changes in topology, a natural question is that of appropriate mathematical descriptions that provide an approach to topological transitions of thin surfaces. Here, we suggest a general intrinsic framework coupling morphogen organization to surface geometry. We propose a minimal geometric model in which smoothing competes with morphogen-induced deformation to regulate shape, while loss of this balance can bring a surface toward a topological transition via neck constriction. A simple dynamical model coupling a scalar field to the surface metric reveals two mechanisms: gradient-driven constriction at steep morphogen transitions and curvature-driven constriction near localized morphogen peaks. For frozen morphogen profiles in simple axisymmetric examples, the gradient-driven route gives exact algebraic contraction, while the curvature-driven route gives local exponential contraction.

items.title: Experimental Evidence for MeV Undulator Radiation Generated by Ultrarelativistic Positrons in a Periodically Bent Crystal
items.summary: We report evidence for undulator radiation generated by ultrarelativistic positrons in a large-amplitude, long-period crystalline undulator. A pattern of Si$_3$N$_4$ stressors periodically bend the (110) planes of a Silicon crystal with a geometry measured independently by x-ray diffraction. Under planar alignment, the forward energy loss showed a localized excess at $6.8 \pm 0.3$~MeV, matching the predictions of simulations. Experimental results also indicate that an intense positron beam could make the undulator competitive in brilliance with state-of-the-art inverse-Compton gamma-ray sources.

items.title: Cumulus parameterization controls simulated rainfall more than microphysics, but not at heavy thresholds: a 3 * 2 factorial WRF study over the Western Himalaya
items.summary: Rainfall forecasts over the Western Himalaya remain poor, and the relative contributions of the cumulus and microphysics parameterizations to that error are not well constrained.

items.title: Boundary-layer scheme selection outweighs microphysics in WRF simulations of the August 2018 Kerala extreme rainfall event
items.summary: Because precipitation is regulated by intricate interactions between topography, cloud microphysics,cumulus convection, radiation, and boundary-layer processes, it is still difficult to accurately simulate orographically enhanced monsoon rainfall over the Western Ghats.

items.title: Stochastic Failure Dynamics in a Model Peptidoglycan Mesh under Hydrolysis and Mechanical Loading
items.summary: We develop a minimal stochastic-mechanical model for failure dynamics of the Gram-negative peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall under blocked growth and continued hydrolysis. The cell wall is modelled as a collection of load-bearing cross-sections, with random number of cross-links in each such cross-section, around a fixed degree of cross-linking. To understand failure dynamics of the cell wall under antibacterial agents which prevent insertion of fresh PG material, peptide bonds are progressively excised by hydrolases, while insertion/formation of new bonds is blocked. We compare and contrast rupture dynamics in no-load and load-activated regimes, using extreme value theory and stochastic simulations, deriving limiting laws for system failure in both the long-cell and large crosslinking limits. For a cross-section with many bonds, the mean failure time grows only log- arithmically with bond number, giving diminishing returns from additional cross-linking. In the no-load case, the centered failure time converges to a Gumbel law, though crucially, load changes the centered distribution and accelerates the final stages of collapse. In long cells, failure follows a weakest-link Weibull-type scaling controlled by the least cross-linked regions, with mechanical load reducing the failure-time scale without changing the weakest-link exponent. The fraction of bonds removed before failure tends to zero, showing that collapse can remain highly localized even while the global cross-linking degree stays high. Slowing down growth and other cellular functions is a typical antibiotic escape mechanism for bacteria and in this context, we show that, hydrolase down-regulation uniformly rescales the failure-time distribution and delays collapse, but does not remove the load-induced preference for rupture in weakened regions.

items.title: Blind spatially varying PSF estimation for fluorescence microscopy
items.summary: Optical aberrations degrade fluorescence microscopy images and measuring the underlying point spread function (PSF) often requires dedicated acquisitions or isolated emitters. Here we introduce DeepBlur, a neural network that estimates spatially varying two-dimensional PSFs directly from single images of biological structures. Trained entirely on physical simulations spanning aberrations, illumination and noise, it adapts to diverse imaging conditions without requiring user-supplied optical parameters. Using a deformable mirror, we acquire 1,290 images and assess blind PSF estimates against independent references. DeepBlur estimates agree closely with these references and improve deconvolution of experimentally aberrated images. Local PSF estimation also enables correction of spatially varying defocus and improves random-illumination super-resolution reconstruction in biological tissue. Available through DeepInv, a napari plugin and a web demonstration, DeepBlur can be readily integrated into computational microscopy workflows.

items.title: Fewer Fractions, Equieffective Plans: An optimization framework based on equieffective dose
items.summary: Background: Non-standard fractionation requires caution before clinical use, and planners often need to manually modify the prescription and dose constraints for non-linear biological effects. Purpose: To develop an extension within a treatment planning system that enables the generation of hypofractionated plans based on equieffective dose, $EQD_{n_{ref}}$, for an alternative fractionation deliverable in $n$ fractions, such that it is equieffective with the reference fractionation for a specified biological endpoint. Methods: A research build of RayStation v2025 was extended to optimize $EQD_{n_{ref}}$ plans. This study used anonymized data from three head and neck patients. $\text{CTV}_p$ and $\text{CTV}_n$ were prescribed 70 Gy and 54 Gy in 35 fractions. Targets, spinal cord, and brainstem were robustly optimized for $\pm3.5$% density and $\pm3.0$ mm setup uncertainties. For each patient, hypofractionated plans were created with 34, 32, 30, and 25 fractions. Sensitivity analysis evaluated the impact of $α/β$ uncertainty. Results: All equieffective hypofractionated plans maintained target coverage and met mandatory clinical goals for organs-at-risk (OARs). Compared to standard fractionation, DVH parameters indicated an average $ΔEQD_{n_{ref}}$ <0.2 Gy for $\text{CTV}_p$ and no difference for $\text{CTV}_n$. For parallel OARs, the median mean-dose difference between hypofractionation (to 30 fractions) and standard fractionation was generally <1% of the prescribed dose. $α/β$ uncertainty produced the greatest variation in the 25-fraction regimen, with absolute $ΔEQD_{n_{ref}}$ up to 0.88 Gy for targets and up to 0.63 Gy for the spinal cord and brainstem. Conclusions: An $EQD_{n_{ref}}$-based framework can generate equieffective hypofractionated plans, making it feasible to reduce fractions without substantially deviating from existing clinical protocols.

items.title: Tunable Terahertz Bandpass Filter based on the Photonic Emulation of a 2DEG Interferometer through the Geometric Phase of Light
items.summary: Terahertz frequencies are expected to become a key player in next-generation wireless communications. For this transition to occur seamlessly, tunable bandpass filters for channel selection are essential. However, conventional Fabry-Pérot cavity-based bandpass filters face inherent limitations. Specifically, their tunability is restricted by physical constraints, such as the maximum achievable mirror separation. In this work, drawing inspiration from electronic interferometers, we demonstrate a continuously tunable bandpass filter operating near 0.3 THz by exploiting the geometric phase of light, the Pancharatnam-Berry phase. Our device incorporates intracavity waveplates for polarization control and is described by a mathematical expression analogous to that of the electronic interferometer governed by the Aharonov-Bohm phase, thereby realizing a photonic analogue. Using custom-designed subwavelength waveplates and cavity mirrors, we achieve a finesse of $\mathcal{F}\approx17$, a quality factor of $Q\approx1.5\times10^{3}$, and a resonance linewidth of $Δf_{\mathrm{FWHM}}\approx 200$ MHz. Beyond terahertz communication technology, this system is expected to find applications in fields requiring high frequency resolution, such as spectroscopy.

items.title: Pressure demand and solute replacement in a collagen-plugged bioreactor
items.summary: In a perfusion bioreactor, fresh culture medium enters through a small opening, flows through a collagen plug, and leaves through a second opening. How much pressure is needed to sustain that flow? When fresh medium reaches the outlet, has it also replaced the old medium inside the pores? To answer these questions, we simulated flow and medium replacement in pores traced from a collagen image. The flow simulations and curved-channel theory show how narrow, winding passages concentrate resistance. We used that resistance to estimate the plug permeability and found that the modeled plug accounts for most of the pressure drop across the chamber. Feeding through small openings adds to that demand because the flow must spread through the plug and converge again at the outlet. At the same flow rate, this requires about seven times the pressure needed with uniform feeding across the plug faces. Pore shape also affects how closely the outlet signal tracks replacement in the interior. In most runs, the interior reaches 99% replacement before the outlet does. A slowly exchanging side pocket can reverse that order by retaining old medium while fresh medium passes through the main channel. In the strongest case, the interior takes nearly three times as long as the outlet to reach the same replacement threshold.

items.title: Theory of Observability of Voigt-Wave Propagation in a Homogeneous Dielectric Material
items.summary: A Voigt wave can propagate in a dissipative anisotropic dielectric material when a 4$\times$4 propagation matrix is defective, as happens for a uniform plane wave along a singular axis, and the field depends on the propagation distance linearly as well as exponentially. Whether it is observable outside a slab of that material generally depends on whether the defectiveness is inherited by the 2$\times$2 reflection and transmission matrices, which are extracted from the 2$\times$2 blocks of a 4$\times$4 transfer matrix that relates the fields at the two faces of the slab. Explicit tests exist for each type of defectiveness, and a counting argument shows that excitation and observability co-occur at oblique incidence only for isolated combinations of constitutive parameters and slab thickness. Normal incidence is exceptional: Voigt-wave excitation then generally implies a defective transmission matrix for almost all thicknesses, which explains Voigt's 1902 experiment on andalusite. Numerical searches for andalusite, $β$-gallium oxide, terbium orthoaluminate in a magnetostatic field, and hexagonal boron nitride show that a Voigt wave may be excited without being observable and that a defective reflection or transmission matrix need not signal the excitation of a Voigt wave.

items.title: Comprehensive In Situ Characterization of Amorphous Solid Water Films with COSPINU2 set-up: Optical Properties, Density, Morphology, and Restructuring Dynamics
items.summary: Amorphous solid water (ASW) dominates interstellar ice mantles, but its porosity, density, optical response, and mechanical stability depend sensitively on how the ice is grown. Here, we present the characterization capabilities of COSPINU2, a cryogenic ultra-high-vacuum set-up designed to prepare and diagnose water ice films under controlled background and doser-assisted deposition conditions. The instrument combines a calibrated gas-handling line, near- and mid-infrared Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, HeNe interferometry, broad-beam optical imaging, and quadrupole mass spectrometry. We demonstrate how these complementary diagnostics provide a coherent description of ASW films grown between 10K and 150K. For background-grown ices, a dual-angle interferometric method is used to retrieve refractive indices near 632 nm, while near-infrared interference fringes provide thickness calibration. The results show that lower deposition temperatures and higher growth rates produce films with lower refractive indices and stronger dangling-OH infrared signatures, consistent with the formation of more porous ASW. We also show that pressure-based density estimates are unreliable in the background geometry because cryopumping decouple chamber pressure from the local substrate flux. For doser-grown films, optical interference imaging allows reconstruction of dome-shaped thickness profiles and estimation of effective densities. Finally, sudden restructuring events are observed in thick (above 2 micrometers), low-temperature porous ASW films, evidenced by abrupt changes in interferometric contrast, optical scattering, and dangling-OH features. These results establish COSPINU2 as a versatile platform for quantitative water-ice characterization and provide the physical baseline required for future studies of infrared irradiation and optical constants of interstellar ice analogues.

items.title: CLM-JAX v3.2.46: a differentiable, GPU-accelerated land surface model numerically indistinguishable from the Community Land Model 5.0
items.summary: The original Fortran implementation of the Community Land Model version 5.0 (CLM5.0) primarily targets CPUs and does not support GPU computation or automatic differentiation. We present CLM-JAX, a land surface model implemented in Python, based on the CLM5.0 BGC-Crop configuration in the Community Earth System Model version 2.1.3 (CESM2.1.3). CLM-JAX retains the original subgrid hierarchy, parameterizations and coupling among energy, water, carbon, nitrogen and crop processes, runs on CPUs and GPUs, and supports gradient backpropagation through multi-step time integration. Using floating-point perturbations of order $10^{-14}$ in the initial state, we construct a stringent ensemble baseline of CLM's own differences and evaluate the numerical consistency of CLM-JAX for 32 variables over five years of continuous global simulation during 2019-2023. CLM-JAX errors relative to CLM generally lie below this ensemble baseline. On a single NVIDIA A800 GPU, CLM-JAX requires 0.7692 s per model hour, yielding sustained integration speedups of 4.04 and 2.57 over CLM compiled with gfortran and ifort, respectively, on 64 CPU cores. In the gradient test, the objective function is the first-layer soil temperature at step 100 (50 h), and its gradient with respect to the initial soil temperature field of all model layers is obtained by backpropagation through the 100 time steps. With converged central finite differences as references, 95.79% of the 84,254 nonzero references have relative errors no greater than 1% and 98.22% have matching signs, with median and 90th-percentile relative errors of $5.862\times10^{-7}$% and $3.578\times10^{-4}$%, respectively. The differentiability of CLM-JAX provides a basis for gradient-based applications, such as end-to-end parameter optimization and four-dimensional variational data assimilation.

items.title: Why do single photons produce interference fringes? The phase of a mode and the phase of a state
items.summary: If the phase of a photon-number state is completely undetermined, how can single photons, sent one at a time through a two-slit apparatus, build up interference fringes? These lecture notes answer this question from first principles. Starting from Maxwell's equations, we expand the field in vector modes, quantize it, and introduce the quantity measured by a photodetector. We then show that the word ``phase'' refers to two different things: the phase of a mode, fixed by the optical setup, and the phase of the quantum state that excites the mode. Only the first determines the fringes. All calculations are given in full, and problems with solutions are included.

items.title: Arbitrarily Weak Losses Destroy Fractal Bandstructure in Temporal Fibonacci Quasicrystals
items.summary: Lossless photonic crystals with weak refractive index contrasts block limited frequencies. However, the same materials arranged in a non-periodic Fibonacci quasicrystal block all but infinitely rare fractally-distributed frequencies. Similar analysis shows that weak quasiperiodic refractive index variation in time should achieve infinitely broadband gain. We demonstrate that any small experimental losses immediately destroy this effect. Our methods also provide smoothness and approximation theorems for the localisation lengths central to topology in spatial problems.

items.title: SCO-Hyper-Meta-Double-GroupNN: A Double-Group SU(2) Hyper-/Meta-Graph Neural Network for Cooperative Spin-Crossover Potential Energy Surfaces
items.summary: Learning potential energy surfaces for magnetic materials requires resolving coupled local spin manifolds and geometric frustration. We introduce SCO-Hyper-Meta-Double-GroupNN, a geometry-only architecture combining a pretrained O(3)-equivariant backbone with SU(2) spinor Hamiltonians and cooperative hyper-/meta-graph interactions. Analytic thermal spinor density matrices provide non-polynomial two- and three-body structural invariants, while frustrated-triangle hyperedges and a multi-shell sideway gate couple geometric representations to local spin manifolds. A variationally consistent, doubly-centered zero-gauge free-energy functional couples multiplet occupations and signed spin orientations, yielding conservative autograd forces without spin inputs at inference. On a first-principles Co-Cr-Ni benchmark comprising 346 training and 59 held-out validation supercells across crystalline, amorphous, glassy, and liquid regimes, compact models with 56k-77k parameters outperform a 207k-parameter spin-conditioned magnetic MACE baseline. Energy MAE decreases by 37-44%, reaching 3.82 versus 6.83 meV/atom, and force MAE decreases by 10.8-14.2 meV/Angstrom, reaching 165.8-169.2 versus 180.0 meV/Angstrom. The models preserve Kramers degeneracy to within $6\times10^{-15}$ eV, predict equilibrium local magnetic moments from geometry alone with an absolute-moment MAE of $0.181\,μ_B$, and support stable molecular dynamics up to 2,200 K. This framework integrates local spinor symmetry and cooperative magnetic interactions into geometry-only interatomic potentials.

items.title: Impact of Cumulus Parameterization and Cloud Microphysics on WRF Simulation of an Extreme Rainfall Event over Maharashtra, India: A 3 by 3 Factorial Assessment
items.summary: Simulating extreme monsoon rainfall over the Konkan coast and Western Ghats remains challenging at 9 km resolution, where convection is partly resolved and partly parameterised. This study evaluates the sensitivity of Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulations of the 5-7 July 2026 Maharashtra rainfall event to cumulus and cloud microphysics schemes. Nine simulations employed a 3 x 3 factorial design combining WSM6, WDM6 and Thompson microphysics with Kain-Fritsch, Tiedtke and Grell-Freitas cumulus schemes. Rainfall was evaluated against IMD 0.25-degree gridded observations, with IMERG and ERA5 as additional references. A descriptive factorial decomposition showed that cumulus parameterisation accounted for 97.3% of across-experiment variation in mean rainfall, 88.2% in RMSE and 84.7% in spatial correlation, while microphysics contributed 2.0%, 2.1% and 9.3%, respectively. Kain-Fritsch produced the highest spatial correlations (0.533-0.581) but substantially overestimated rainfall. Tiedtke achieved the smallest mean biases and RMSE, although compensating regional errors concealed a 28-34% rainfall deficit over the Konkan-Ghats belt and substantial underestimation on 7 July. Grell-Freitas showed large wet biases and relatively high RMSE. All nine simulations displaced the event-total rainfall maximum approximately 140-195 km northward. WSM6-Tiedtke achieved the lowest RMSE, whereas Thompson-Kain-Fritsch better represented the rainfall spatial pattern. The findings demonstrate that, for this event and fixed model configuration, cumulus parameterisation exerted substantially greater influence on simulated rainfall than cloud microphysics. However, a single-event, single-member experimental design does not establish a universally optimal physics configuration.

items.title: Machine-Learning-Enhanced Mapping of Activity and Selectivity in CO$_2$ Hydrogenation across Metal-Alloy Surfaces
items.summary: Adsorption energy distributions (AEDs) have emerged as a powerful and increasingly adopted descriptor for catalytic performance in high-entropy alloys and, more recently, in conventional metallic alloy nanocrystal catalysts. By accounting for diverse adsorption sites and crystallographic facets, AEDs more fully represent nanoparticle-based catalytic surfaces and show strong promise for accelerating rational design and discovery of heterogeneous catalysts, especially for CO$_2$ hydrogenation. However, previous high-throughput screenings have not provided simultaneous facet-level insight into catalytic activity, product selectivity, and thermodynamic stability. Here, we implement and extend the AED framework to individual crystallographic facets, combining facet-resolved adsorption fingerprints with Wulff-derived facet abundances and an interpretable latent-space analysis of C1-product selectivity. We employ universal machine-learned force fields trained on Open Catalyst data to compute adsorption energies across 226 experimentally observed metals, binary alloys, and previously unexplored ternary alloys, encompassing $\approx$1.4 million adsorption configurations on $>$2,600 crystallographically distinct surfaces. Using distribution-based similarity analysis and principal component analysis of AED moments, we identify composition-facet combinations with adsorption landscapes associated with activity and qualitative selectivity trends toward C1 products such as methanol and methane. Our framework links surface structure to adsorption-based catalytic trends, providing experimentally testable composition-facet candidates for further investigation and validation.

items.title: Site-Resolved Optical Spectroscopy of Thulium in Solid Argon
items.summary: We utilize the high resolution of the ground state transition ${}^2\mathrm{F}_{7/2} \leftrightarrow {}^2\mathrm{F}_{5/2}$ in thulium atoms isolated in solid argon to perform excitation-emission spectroscopy. Decomposition of the excitation-emission spectrum reveals 6 absorption-emission profiles, which are attributed to multiple trapping sites in the host matrix. Comparison with vacuum transition energies shows large matrix-induced shifts for $\mathrm{s}\rightarrow\mathrm{p}$ transitions, whereas $\mathrm{f} \rightarrow \mathrm{d}$ transitions remain close to their free-atom energies. A single site exhibiting strong emission at 560nm is investigated and a three-photon excitation pathway is determined as a possible origin of the high energy 560nm light. Additionally, for long-lived levels belonging to the $\mathrm{f}^{12}\mathrm{d}$ configuration, narrow, crystal-field split absorption lines are identified. Matrix effects are important for establishing the mechanism behind the observed spectra and long $\mathrm{f}^{12}\mathrm{d}$ lifetimes.

items.title: A Monolithic Fully Eulerian Lattice Boltzmann Framework for Fluid--Structure Interaction with Neo-Hookean Elastic Solids
items.summary: We present a fully Eulerian, monolithic lattice Boltzmann method for fluid--structure interaction with incompressible neo-Hookean solids at unequal densities, and use it to compute the Turek--Hron FSI2 and FSI3 benchmarks on a single Cartesian grid. A pressure-based kinetic scheme advances the mixture momentum, a polynomial MTHINC reconstruction transports the solid volume fraction with closed-form fluxes, and the left Cauchy--Green tensor gives the elastic stress; all updates are explicit and local. Because the density is transported independently of the populations, two corrections are introduced. A lattice-link correction makes uniform translation an exact discrete solution for any density ratio, which is verified to round-off up to $ρ_s/ρ_f=1000$. A pressure-mode correction, derived from an asymptotic analysis of the scheme, removes the frame-dependent defect that otherwise causes a secular drift of the solid mass. The verification separates the two sources of error: the scheme is second-order accurate towards the diffuse-interface solution at fixed interface thickness, and first-order towards the sharp-interface solution when the thickness scales with the grid, as predicted by an estimate of the interfacial truncation error. The method reproduces a deformable disk in Taylor--Green and lid-driven-cavity flows, and the FSI3 and FSI2 benchmarks at density ratios of one and ten.

items.title: PEPSKit.jl: A Julia package for projected entangled-pair state simulations
items.summary: We present PEPSKit$.$jl, a Julia package for simulating two-dimensional quantum many-body systems with infinite projected entangled-pair states (iPEPS). PEPSKit$.$jl builds on the TensorKit$.$jl package for tensor computations and provides high-level algorithms for iPEPS simulations that support both Abelian and non-Abelian symmetries, as well as fermionic systems. This work gives an overview of the main package features, which include support for ground-state, time-evolution, and finite-temperature simulations in systems with different physical symmetries and lattice geometries. These capabilities are illustrated through various examples and technical benchmarks.

items.title: StePPO: Adaptive Step-Size Control for Initial-Value Problems Using Proximal Policy Optimisation
items.summary: ODE solvers are used to model, simulate, and analyse continuous-time systems found in many signal processing applications. Time integration of these initial-value problems is traditionally performed using adaptive embedded Runge--Kutta methods. For proper time-step selection, adaptive solvers accept or reject each candidate step according to a local error estimate. Their efficiency is therefore controlled by the rule that selects the next step size. Classical proportional--integral--derivative (PID) controllers are computationally inexpensive per decision and reliable, but their reactive design can lead to costly numerical solves near stiff transitions. We formulate step-size selection for parametrised IVPs as a Markov decision process and train a continuous-action policy using proximal policy optimisation. The policy processes its observation signals using a deep network while maintaining the embedded solver logic. We evaluate on a decay function, the Van der Pol system, and the Brusselator system at matched tolerances, and compare against a standard PID controller and a multi-scale DeepONet network. We find that the proposed learned policy remains within prescribed error tolerances while reducing the required number of solve steps by up to 60%, achieving a wall-clock time reduction of 58%, for both in- and out-of-distribution settings.

items.title: Backpropagation as Dirac-bracket dynamics of dissipative training
items.summary: Gradient-based training of a parametric model is the motion of a damped particle in the potential set by the loss. Using the Bateman-Galley doubling of the degrees of freedom, which gives dissipative systems an action principle, we write gradient flow, the heavy-ball method and Nesterov's accelerated gradient method as Hamiltonian systems. We show that, within this Hamiltonian description, backpropagation is Dirac evolution. The activations of a feed-forward network are treated as coordinates of phase space, and the layer equations as constraints. These constraints are second class for every architecture, and Hamilton's equations with the resulting Dirac bracket reproduce training with the exact gradient of the loss, although the Hamiltonian contains only the cost of the network output. The Dirac bracket of an activation with the momenta of the parameters is its Jacobian, the inverse of the constraint matrix contains both the forward and the reverse modes of automatic differentiation, and the errors propagated by backpropagation are the Lagrange multipliers of the layer constraints: the constraint forces of a kinematic chain under the load of the cost. These results hold in the full doubled phase space, not only in the physical limit. The network's part of the constraint algebra is the same for every optimizer, Nesterov's look-ahead adds one layer of momentum-dependent constraints that couple the two copies of the doubled system, and gradient flow is obtained by constructing the Dirac bracket in stages. We confirm these statements numerically to machine precision and train a network by integrating the Dirac flow of its constraints, with no backward pass in the computation.

items.title: A European high-capacity 100 MeV-per-nucleon heavy-ion facility for electronics irradiation based at CERN: Conceptual Design Report
items.summary: This proposal presents a conceptual design for a European high-energy heavy-ion facility dedicated to electronics radiation-effects testing, directly addressing the critical challenges of global beam time shortages and energy limitations in existing facilities. Aligned with the HORIZON-CL4-2026-SPACE-03-85 call under Horizon Europe's Cluster 4 (Digital, Industry, and Space), the facility will enhance European sovereignty in space technology by providing approximately 1,900 additional hours of high-energy heavy-ion beam time annually, an increase of about 50% in the total heavy-ion beam time currently available in Europe for single-event-effect testing, and by extending the accessible ion energy range up to 100 MeV/nucleon, significantly improving penetration capabilities for state-of-the-art electronics testing. The facility will leverage CERN's ion injector chain up to the Low Energy Ion Ring (LEIR) synchrotron, adding a second ion source, a dedicated slow-extraction system, a transfer line and a user experimental area. The project timeline includes a pre-technical-design (pre-TDR) phase and a technical design phase leading to a Technical Design Report (TDR), followed by infrastructure and hardware production, installation, commissioning, and user operations. Funding is envisaged through a collaborative framework involving CERN and the European Union, with the aim of ensuring sustainable deployment and long-term operational success.

items.title: Uphill Diffusion in Yukawa Plasmas
items.summary: In a fluid mixture of many species an individual species can diffuse toward higher concentration without any external driving force because its flux is coupled to the gradients of other components. Such `uphill diffusion' is well known in the chemical and metallurgy literature but to our knowledge has not been studied for strongly coupled plasmas in neutron star and white dwarf interiors. We have previously developed a semi-analytic diffusion model that accurately predicts diffusion coefficients of individual species in a mixture in equilibrium. Uphill diffusion allows us to test this model out of equilibrium, and also test a generalized Darken relation for predicting diffusivities. We derive an analytic theory and compare to three-component molecular dynamics simulations and find very good agreement. This provides a novel out-of-equilibrium test of the generalization of our diffusion model to arbitrary multi-component mixtures.

items.title: Anti-Collapse Dynamics and the Emergence of Multi-Time-Scale Learning in Recurrent Neural Networks
items.summary: Long-range learning is hard for recurrent networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, because the influence of a past input fades with the lag $\ell$, and if it fades too fast the dependence cannot be learned from finite data. This fade is captured by an envelope $f(\ell)$. An exponential fade makes the data needed to learn a lag-$\ell$ dependence grow exponentially, putting long horizons out of reach; a power-law fade keeps the cost polynomial. We show that the asymptotic decay behavior of $f(\ell)$ is not fixed by the architecture. Instead, it emerges from the coupling between the state dynamics and parameter dynamics, settling into either a collapsed regime (fast, exponential forgetting) or an extended, anti-collapsed regime (slow, power-law forgetting). The intuition is a competition within these coupled dynamics. The systematic part of the training updates pulls long effective time scales back toward the network's typical range, while rare, heavy-tailed fluctuations can push a few far beyond it. When these pushes are strong enough to balance the pull, the extended regime survives. We make this mathematically precise with a coarse-grained stochastic process and derive the explicit threshold above which this balance holds. A single exponent, the spectral exponent~$β$, then governs both the spread of time scales and how slowly the network forgets. Realizing the regime in practice needs one more ingredient: the joint action of the architecture and the optimizer must be able to hold such a broad spread. A network whose capacity to generate broad time-scale spectra is severely constrained still collapses, even when supplied with strong heavy-tailed forcing. Heavy-tailed fluctuations thus act not as noise to be suppressed, but as the mechanism that sustains long-range learning.

items.title: Solitons as conversion events in quadratic crystals
items.summary: In a $χ^{(2)}$ crystal with temporal walk-off and negligible dispersion, signal, idler and pump pulses obey the integrable three-wave interaction. For a pump of intermediate group velocity we describe each soliton as a conversion event: the fusion of a signal--idler pair into a pump pulse, or the decay of a pump pulse, at a definite depth in the crystal. The asymptotic $\mathrm{sech}$ pulses, usually treated with three separate $2\times2$ scattering problems, are the legs of the event, a single pole of the $3\times3$ problem. For one event we give the conversion curve in closed form and the minimum crystal length; for several events, the rule by which they displace each other. A pump pulse is unstable, and its growing mode is the tail of a decay event: a seed carrying a fraction $\varepsilon$ of the photons along this mode makes the pulse decay after $Γ^{-1}\ln(c_+/\varepsilon)$, with $Γ$ the conversion rate and $c_+$ of order one. Unmatched signal and idler pulses form the resonance of Kaup, Reiman and Bers; we show that it is a fusion followed by a decay, each within a conversion length, and give its pump photon number in closed form. Since the delay between the input pulses sets the depth of the vertex, these quantities can be read on the output face of a single crystal; we give the scales for periodically poled KTiOPO$_4$.

items.title: Variational approach to droplet motion on uneven solid surfaces, including contact line dynamics and evaporation
items.summary: We show how dynamical equations for liquid films and drops on uneven surfaces, including contact line dynamics and evaporation/condensation effects, may be formulated as a variational dynamics, generated via Onsager's variational principle. The theory applies in the isothermal overdamped-dynamics limit. We apply this general approach to obtain several well-known results on contact line dynamics and to study drops pinning and sliding on inclined corrugated surfaces. This approach constructs the dynamical equations starting from the free energy of the system and therefore has the advantage that it naturally incorporates the correct equilibrium properties.

items.title: Full-waveform inversion with adaptive anisotropic Gaussian primitives
items.summary: Reparameterizing the velocity model has emerged as an effective way to regularize full-waveform inversion (FWI) and reduce its sensitivity to the starting model. Existing parameterizations, however, either fix the position and shape of every basis function in advance, as in grids and splines, or control the spatial structure of their updates only indirectly through the shared weights of a neural network. We propose Gauss-FWI, which represents the velocity perturbation as a sum of anisotropic Gaussian primitives with learnable amplitudes, centres, scales, and orientations. The basis itself thus adapts to the subsurface. Primitives move onto interfaces, stretch along layers, and rotate with the dip, so model updates follow the geological structure without a hand-designed regularizer. A gradient-energy criterion adds finer zero-amplitude primitives where the data call for more detail, increasing resolution progressively without perturbing the current model. All parameters receive analytic gradients through the adjoint-state method on a fixed simulation grid, so the representation fits into existing FWI workflows and combines directly with frequency continuation. Each primitive keeps an explicit position, extent, and orientation, and the representation Jacobian links the waveform gradient to the resulting model update, which makes the behaviour of the inversion interpretable. In two-dimensional acoustic examples, Gauss-FWI uses about fifty times fewer parameters than implicit FWI and recovers the Marmousi, Overthrust, and BP salt models more accurately than grid, multiscale, B-spline, and implicit parameterizations. It remains accurate under missing low frequencies, noise, and discretization mismatch, and it recovers the main structure from starting models where the other methods fail, such as a linear model without the BP salt body.

items.title: Graph Parameterization for Invariant Manifolds Attached to Quasi-Periodic Tori
items.summary: We develop a high-order Fourier-Taylor graph-parameterization method for computing local invariant manifolds attached to reducible quasi-periodic invariant tori of discrete dynamical systems, with particular emphasis on Poincaré maps. Assuming that the invariant torus and its Floquet reduction are known, we represent the manifold as a graph over a selected spectral subspace and compute its coefficients recursively through jet transport and cohomological equations on the torus. The formulation accommodates stable, unstable, and center spectral selections. For center manifolds, it simultaneously determines the nonlinear reduced dynamics, providing a low-dimensional representation from which nearby invariant objects can be lifted to the original phase space. For real systems with complex-conjugate Floquet multipliers, we derive an equivalent real formulation based on Hermitian symmetry and Krawtchouk transformations. This allows real-valued jet transport while retaining the advantages of complex spectral coordinates in the cohomological solver. The implementation also incorporates inverse dynamics for stable directions, multiple shooting, coordinate scaling, and a posteriori validation tests. Numerical experiments with a quasi-periodically forced pendulum, an oscillating solar sail in the Earth-Moon system, and a simplified solar system model illustrate the construction and its computational properties. In the solar-sail benchmark, the real formulation reduces computation time by approximately a factor of 2.2 compared with the complex implementation.

items.title: A complete phase-field fracture model for brittle materials subjected to thermal shocks
items.summary: Brittle materials subjected to thermal shocks experience strong temperature gradients that in turn give rise to mechanical stresses that can be large enough to induce fracture. This work presents a complete model for phase-field fracture for coupled thermo-mechanical problems, wherein the bulk material properties, the material strength, and the fracture toughness are specified independently. The capabilities of the model are assessed across a wide span of scenarios in thermo-mechanical fracture, from the propagation of large pre-existing cracks to crack nucleation under spatially uniform states of stress. In particular, we revisit the controlled quenching of glass plates, and demonstrate how the model captures experimentally observed crack patterns across a range of thermal loads. Ceramic disks subjected to infrared radiation are also examined, with the model reproducing both straight cracks in notched specimens and branching in intact specimens. Finally, ceramic pellets subjected to rapid power pulses are examined, with the model explaining experimental transitions from intact to fractured pellets and the important role of material strength. The results demonstrate that the complete phase-field model unifies the treatment of distinct fracture scenarios under thermal shock, surpassing classical approaches and enabling more reliable prediction of brittle fracture in extreme environments.

items.title: Quantum theory of electrically levitated nanoparticle-ion systems: Motional dynamics and sympathetic cooling
items.summary: We develop the theory describing the quantum coupled dynamics of the center-of-mass motion of a nanoparticle and an ensemble of ions co-trapped in a dual-frequency linear Paul trap. We first derive analytical expressions for the motional frequencies and classical trajectories of both nanoparticle and ions. We then derive a quantum master equation for the ion-nanoparticle system and quantify the sympathetic cooling of the nanoparticle motion enabled by its Coulomb coupling to a continuously Doppler-cooled ion. We predict that motional cooling down to sub-kelvin temperatures is achievable in state-of-the-art experiments even in the absence of motional feedback and in the presence of micromotion. We then extend our analysis to an ensemble of $N$ ions, predicting a linear increase of the cooling rate as a function of N and motional cooling of the nanoparticle down to tenths of millikelvin in current experimental platforms. Our work establishes the theoretical toolbox needed to explore the ion-assisted preparation of non-Gaussian motional states of levitated nanoparticles.

items.title: Structure-preserving finite element method for the 2D MHD-$α$ turbulence system
items.summary: We propose a structure-preserving finite element method for the two-dimensional MHD-$α$ turbulence model, which filters the transport velocity at a length $α$ while retaining the ideal invariants of the original MHD equations, with the energy replaced by an $α$-dependent energy. The scheme preserves mass conservation and the magnetic Gauss law pointwise and satisfies discrete dissipation laws for the energy, the cross helicity and the mean square magnetic potential, which reduce to exact conservation in the ideal limit. The discrete systems are solved by an augmented Lagrangian preconditioner with monolithic geometric multigrid, observed to be robust with respect to the filter width $α$ and the Reynolds numbers, and to the mesh size for small time steps. The scheme converges at the optimal rates and agrees with a Fourier pseudo-spectral direct simulation of the original MHD equations at the large scales. In under-resolved flows, the unfiltered scheme has no numerical dissipation and accumulates energy at the grid scale. Filtering relieves this accumulation and a larger $α$ gives a more compact spectrum. Long-time simulations reproduce selective decay, including relaxation toward the Arnold-type bound and the inverse cascade of the mean square potential.

items.title: Optimization of a Locally Shielded 16-Channel Transmit Array for Human Brain MRI at 10.5 T via Electromagnetic/Circuit Co-Simulation and Parallel Transmission Strategies
items.summary: Modern neuroimaging and neuroscience increasingly demand high spatial and temporal resolution, driving the use of ultrahigh-field (7 T and above) MRI for improved signal-to-noise ratio. Realizing this advantage depends critically on advanced radiofrequency (RF) and gradient technologies, particularly multi-channel transmit arrays and high-performance head-gradient systems.
