To our knowledge, this is the first Sentaurus-based mixed-mode TCAD implementation for nTrons. We calibrate the model against experimental switching data at six gate currents using a single parameter set. The model achieves an RMS load-current error below 1 $μ$A outside the switching region and switching-current differences of about 1 $μ$A or less. Simulations show that a center gate gives the highest switching sensitivity, while a drain-side gate gives the largest post-switch resistance. Narrower channels switch at lower currents and exhibit higher resistance. Transient and bidirectional bias sweeps capture electrothermal hysteresis, gate-controlled switching latency, and bias-controlled recovery. Simultaneous activation of three gates lowers the switching threshold from about 104 $μ$A with all gates inactive to about 12 $μ$A, demonstrating cooperative suppression of superconductivity. The framework supports the design of nTron geometries, operating conditions, and multi-input architectures.

items.title: Time Travel Paradoxes and Entangled Timelines
items.summary: For time travel to be consistent with the known laws of physics, the resulting paradoxes must be resolved. It has been suggested that the notion of parallel timelines may provide a resolution, by allowing different events to happen in different timelines. However, so far, a concrete mechanism by which parallel timelines can be created has never been satisfactorily formulated in a way that makes the relationships between the timelines clear. In this paper, we propose such a mechanism based on the Everett (many-worlds) interpretation of quantum mechanics. The timelines in our model are variants of the "worlds" of the Everett interpretation that can connect to each other via the time machine. They are created by the entanglement of the time machine with the environment and the resulting decoherence; therefore, we call them "entangled timelines" or E-CTCs. As the entanglement gradually spreads out to additional systems, the timelines spread out as well, providing a local and well-defined mechanism for branching timelines. The E-CTC model is similar to Deutsch's familiar D-CTC model but differs from it mainly by imposing a different consistency condition, based on pure states, which allows the information about the entanglement to be preserved. These differences allow us to create a clearer practical definition of the timelines and avoid some of the surprising consequences of the D-CTC model's non-linear evolution.

items.title: How Many Keys Must a Quantum Computer Break to Take Over a Blockchain? A Quantum Nakamoto Coefficient for Fifteen Proof-of-Stake Networks
items.summary: Blockchains that run on proof of stake, among them Ethereum and Solana, are secured by a vote: a transaction becomes irreversible once computers holding two thirds of the deposited money have signed it. Each signature is made with a secret key whose public counterpart is permanently visible, and a large quantum computer could compute the secret from the public key. We ask a simple question: how many such keys would it have to break to take over the vote? We call the answer the quantum Nakamoto coefficient and measure it on live data from fifteen networks, collected on 15 November 2026. For fourteen of them, 2 to 18 keys are enough to break the network's security guarantee and 7 to 77 to control it outright; at one key every 12 minutes, the pace implied by recent resource estimates, a single quantum computer would defeat the guarantee of any of these networks in less than four hours and take full control in less than sixteen hours. Ethereum is far more robust, but a 2025 change that lets operators merge their deposits into fewer keys has cut the number of keys at its first threshold from about 465,000 to 7,682, a factor of 60. We derive a simple formula for this effect, and another for the small rotating committee on which wallets rely, and confirm both on the data. For fourteen of the fifteen networks, the first large quantum computer would be less than a day away from total control. Their validator signatures should therefore be migrated to post-quantum schemes before such a machine exists, since once it does, the time to respond is measured in hours.

items.title: Point vortex dynamics influenced by the surface motion
items.summary: We study a coupled system of differential equations, which models the dynamics of fluid with a free surface and a point vortex in the body of the fluid. For long surface waves of small amplitude, the effects of the interaction between the waves and the point vortex are modeled within the framework of the Boussinesq regime. It turns out that the solitary waves on the surface are not destroyed by the interaction with the vortex, and, as a matter of fact, the solitary waves remain practically unaffected for a significant range of the vortex strength. As a result, a further simplification of the model is proposed, where the vortex motion under solitons propagating on the surface is determined from a system of decoupled ordinary differential equations.

items.title: Computing hydration free energies and crystalline solubility of drug-like molecules with MACE
items.summary: Accurate prediction of thermodynamic solubility is critical in drug discovery, where it influences oral bioavailability and drives decisions in formulation chemistry. First-principles calculations of intrinsic solubility offer the potential to achieve superior generalization to existing direct, data-driven predictors, which often suffer significant performance degradation outside of their training distribution. Whilst free energy perturbation calculations provide a rigorous framework to estimate these quantities, their accuracy is typically limited by the quality of the empirical force field used. In this work, we present a computational workflow driven by the MACE family of machine learning interatomic potentials to compute the solubility of neutral drug-like molecules. We introduce $λ$-MACE, a potential optimised for condensed-phase free energy calculations, which enables hydration free energy calculations at experimental accuracy on an evaluation set of 70 compounds from the FreeSolv database selected for their relevance to medicinal chemistry. We further combine these hydration free energy calculations with sublimation free energy calculations to predict crystalline solubility given a known experimental crystal structure, on an additional set of 10 compounds. We achieve state-of-the-art performance for each leg of the calculation, with experimental accuracy for the hydration leg, and accuracy competitive with industry-standard DFT for the sublimation leg. However, the overall errors after combining both legs lead to accuracy of 1.53 log units. This is significantly above the experimental accuracy (0.17-0.6 log units). Closing this gap will require substantially tighter accuracy in each leg, on the order of half of chemical accuracy (0.5 kcal/mol), with crystalline thermodynamics the hardest remaining challenge.

items.title: Engineered Simultaneity: The Physical Impossibility of Consolidated Price Discovery Across Spacelike-Separated Exchanges
items.summary: We define engineered simultaneity: the construction of a system that requires temporal comparison of events at spacelike-separated locations, implements this comparison via an implicit simultaneity convention, and represents the result as an objective measurement rather than a conventional choice. We show that the National Best Bid and Offer (NBBO) -- the cornerstone of U.S. equity markets -- is an instance of engineered simultaneity. The NBBO requires determining "current" prices across exchanges whose spatial separation places their price events outside each other's light cones. Special relativity proves that the temporal ordering of such events is frame-dependent: there exist inertial reference frames in which the NBBO differs from the value reported by the Securities Information Processor. The impossibility is not approximate; it is exact and unavoidable within the causal structure of Minkowski spacetime, and general relativity and indefinite causal order only compound it. We formalize the argument using the causal precedence relation and connect it to Lamport's theorem on distributed ordering. The operational form of the result needs no moving observers: the NBBO depends on where it is computed, and every participant who is not at the consolidation point holds a different one. The same construction recurs inside a single exchange, where orders are stamped at a perimeter and sorted by the stamp. Read as a practitioner suggests, as a bound on the worst-case error of distributed price discovery, the NBBO is defensible, and we propose that it be published as one. We separate what a central market is for (aggregating supply and demand) from what the latency race is about (sequencing arrivals), note that races of this kind cost about $5 billion a year in global equities, and record that in June 2026 the SEC proposed to rescind the order protection rule that makes the NBBO binding.

items.title: Data Unfolding: From Problem Formulation to Result Assessment
items.summary: Experimental data in particle and nuclear physics, particle astrophysics, and radiation protection dosimetry are collected using experimental facilities that consist of a complex system of sensors, electronics, and software. Measured spectra or cross sections are considered as Probability Density Functions (PDFs) that deviate from true PDFs due to resolution, bias, and efficiency effects. Unfolding is viewed as a procedure for estimating an unknown true PDF. Reliable estimates of the true PDF are necessary for testing theoretical models, comparing results from different experiments, and combining results from various research endeavors. Both external and internal quality assessment methods can be applied for this purpose. In some cases, external criteria exist to evaluate deconvolution quality. A typical example is the deconvolution of a blurred image, where the sharpness of the restored image serves as an indicator of quality. However, defining such external criteria can be challenging, particularly when a measurement has not been performed previously. This paper discusses various internal criteria for assessing the quality of the results independently of external information, as well as factors that influence the quality of the unfolded distribution.

items.title: Gaussian priors from nonlinear PDEs with the semiclassical approximation
items.summary: Probabilistic numerical methods for partial differential equations (PDE) combines the governing physics with observations to treat solving the PDE as a Bayesian inverse problem. This allows techniques to quantify the uncertainty in the field reconstruction under model-form error. In the majority of cases, a Gaussian prior is assigned to the field of interest, and Bayes's theorem in the infinite-dimensional setting is used to derive the posterior. While Gaussians have been shown to be well-suited for linear PDEs, a similar treatment for nonlinear PDEs remains open-ended. In this work, study the use of the semiclassical approximation to construct Gaussian priors from variational energies or integrated square residuals for probabilistic numerics. The prior is derived by expanding the PDE energy about a stable solution and uncovering a Gaussian form. We then analyze the different characteristics of the resulting priors as they pertain to the inverse problem. In particular, we find that the covariance operator is given by the inverse of the Hessian of the energy whose associated Cameron-Martin space is the solution space of the PDE. We also find that the prior responds to model-form error by sharpening or flattening itself depending on the distance between the ground truth and the solution of the assumed model.

items.title: Electrical grid stabilisation through agent strategies : a mean-field game approach
items.summary: We propose and solve a minimal model based on mean-field game theory to study decentralized power consumption strategies to stabilize power grids. The mean-field Kuramoto description of an electrical network is coupled to agents with anticipatory capacity for decision making in energy consumption. Each agent minimizes an individual cost which includes both a financial part (cost induce by consumption and by power reservation) imposed by a central authority, and a (personal) non-monetary part. This elementary model of active oscillators is exactly solvable in the steady state regime. We show that the synchronized regime of the network can be significantly extended by the game.

items.title: Basin-Scale Nonlinear Dynamics of Thermohaline Ocean Circulation. Part I: Theory
items.summary: Earth's thermohaline ocean circulation may support multiple equilibria and abrupt transitions. Similar bifurcation structures for different ocean models suggest common underlying dynamics across the model hierarchy. Here we propose a unifying framework from tracer conservation, in which surface fluxes are balanced by dissipative and advective tracer transport. We express this flux balance through a large-scale tracer gradient and a transport efficiency that measures how strongly circulation displaces the tracer field from its no-flow "conductive" state. The flux balance quantifies the transport contributions that sustain each circulation state and give rise to abrupt transitions. In a three-dimensional ocean-basin model, we find nonlinear salinity advection dominates the collapse threshold and linear dissipation dominates the recovery threshold. Temperature has additional dissipation from surface restoring, making thermal fluxes more dissipation-dominated than salinity fluxes. The tracer contrasts and boundary layers that a given circulation generates produce distinct transport regimes, approximately quadratic in circulation strength for weak flow and linear for strong flow. With a simple circulation closure, the flux balance reduces to longstanding box-model bifurcation results for the weak and strong flow regimes. Thus, by expressing thermohaline bifurcations through basin-scale transport, this framework connects box-model insight to the continuous equations. Furthermore, as this framework exposes the transport processes that balance a changing forcing, it provides constraints on a thermohaline ocean state and its trend toward tipping that overturning strength alone does not. In Part II, we develop flux-balance closures to forecast such tipping points.

items.title: Dressed Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory: Opening and Closing a Pandora's box
items.summary: Dressed time-dependent density functional theory (DTDDFT) has been shown to overcome the inability of adiabatic TDDFT to describe excitation energies and oscillator strengths of double-excitation character, however, it is far from being a black-box method. Here, we outline and address several operational issues while benchmarking the approach on a range of molecules. We define a protocol to determine whether an excitation from adiabatic TDDFT needs a double-excitation correction, without requiring a priori knowledge of the state, and which Kohn-Sham states to build the frequency-dependent DTDDFT matrix from. We present an 'undownfolding' that replaces this frequency-dependent matrix by a linear frequency-independent one in a larger space, eliminating ambiguities in the iterative procedure required to diagonalize the former. We compare the performance of DTDDFT for both excitation energies and oscillator strengths, as measured by an approximate metric for their single-excitation character, for different choices of the underlying adiabatic density functional approximation, with and without employing the Tamm-Dancoff approximation, for molecular excitations predicted by wavefunction methods to have either partial or genuine double-excitation character. We propose a correction to DTDDFT to account for missing dynamical correlation that is removed in the truncation procedure inherent in the method, and discuss the possibility of unphysical imaginary frequencies reminiscent of the 'triplet instability' that may arise. We provide benchmark data for butadiene, hexatriene, octatetraene, cyclopentadiene, acrolein, naphthalene, ethylene, borole, and cyclopentadienone. In some cases, DTDDFT predicts frequencies with about as much accuracy as the same underlying adiabatic TDDFT predicts for the constituent and near-lying single excitations.

items.title: Ultrasensitive, universal single-ion nanodetector
items.summary: In this paper, a carbon nanotube (CNT) based single-ion detector is proposed and its performance is evaluated with atomistic quantum transport models. The sensor can detect any ion type without molecule-specific functionalization and allows for continuous real-time ion monitoring. A single ion temporarily changes the operating principle of the sensor's CNT field-effect transistor into a resonant tunneling diode. The concrete device example of this paper showed a source-drain current increase of 5 orders of magnitude induced by a single ion.

items.title: Butterfly Effect in Kinetic Plasma Turbulence
items.summary: The butterfly effect is a fundamental process in chaotic systems, but it has not previously been characterized in detail for a collisionless turbulent plasma. In this work, we apply particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations of driven turbulence to study the emergence of the butterfly effect from a small initial perturbation to the simulated particles. In particular, we compare pairs of (baseline and perturbed) simulations that differ only by a localized initial perturbation (down to the single-particle level). We find that the effect of the localized perturbation spreads radially throughout the PIC simulation, causing a difference between each simulation pair that is exponentially amplified over time within the affected region. The fields, including the electric current density, eventually become statistically decorrelated. We construct an analytical model combining spatial expansion with exponential amplification to approximate the early-time evolution. Varying the initial perturbation primarily affects the early-time evolution, while having little effect on the final, decorrelated state. We describe parameter scans with varying plasma beta and temperature (covering sub-relativistic and ultra-relativistic regimes). Our results show that remarkably small perturbations will grow to decorrelate each pair of simulations within a few dynamical times; the imposed perturbation can no longer be resolved once it falls below the numerical precision floor set by the machine precision. These results confirm that the butterfly effect is very strong and robust in a collisionless plasma, with implications for the predictability of turbulent plasma systems.

items.title: Lossless propagation of gain-compensated graphene plasmons
items.summary: Graphene plasmons offer strong electromagnetic confinement and electrical tunability, but dissipation in the graphene sheet limits their propagation. Here, we investigate how optical gain in the surrounding dielectrics can compensate these losses in single- and double-layer graphene. Starting from the full electromagnetic boundary conditions and a finite-temperature graphene conductivity, we derive the compensation condition for a single sheet and the separate optical and acoustic dispersion relations for two coupled sheets. We show that the required gain depends both on material loss and on where the gain is placed. When gain is present throughout the dielectric environment, the two double-layer modes have nearly identical compensation thresholds. When it is confined to the spacer or the outer claddings, their thresholds separate because the modes overlap differently with each region. Full-wave finite-element simulations reproduce the predicted branches and field symmetries and show a strong suppression of attenuation together with a substantial increase in propagation length. The analysis also identifies the range over which a local conductivity provides a controlled description. These results show how the spatial distribution of gain can be used to control the compensation thresholds of the optical and acoustic graphene plasmons.

items.title: Anomalous scaling of coalescence in a Hele-Shaw cell
items.summary: We investigate the merging of two drops between two narrowly spaced plates, a so-called Hele-Shaw cell. For this, we solve the Hele-Shaw equations in two dimensions, driven by surface tension, focusing on early times after initial reconnection. Combining numerical simulations with theory, we show that the coalescence dynamics are self-similar at early times, with the size of the contact region between the drops growing as $t^{3/13}$. We find this power law using a matched asymptotic analysis, which reveals a complex geometry consisting of a small bubble that gets entrained between the drops as they come together. These predictions match perfectly to our simulations, and agree with the most recent experimental data.

items.title: On the binding and stability of CeO2 molecules on low-index Au surfaces
items.summary: Many multi-phase thin films grown by self-assembly involve co-deposition of both metallic and oxide phases that grow into the same film. Under such conditions, the oxide species may be present in stoichiometric molecular form on the surface of the metallic phase. Quantifying the stability, binding, and diffusion of such molecular oxide states on metallic surfaces is critical for understanding self-assembly. In this work, we investigate the binding and stability of CeO2 molecules on Au surfaces using spin-polarized density functional theory calculations. Specifically, we examine how the configuration of the CeO2 molecule, its binding energy and binding free energy, structural stability, effective charge, and projected electronic density of states vary among various binding sites on Au(001), Au(110), and Au(111) surfaces. Molecular CeO2 was found to be more favorable on all Au surfaces than its atomic constituents. It was also found that the bent CeO2 molecule configuration is more stable than the linear counterpart, with the Ce atom on the hollow site and the O atoms on the top sites. In addition, the configurations of the CeO2 molecule on Au surfaces with a binding energy around or weaker than -1 eV were found to have a low probability of existence above room temperature. Furthermore, the charge transfer was found to occur in such a way that the CeO2 molecule becomes polarized on all surfaces, but the polarization is stronger only for the strongly bonded states on Au(001) and Au(110) surfaces. Finally, three different cases of how the CeO2 molecule binds to Au(001), Au(110), and Au(111) were identified: case 1: chemisorption with symmetric bonds, case 2: chemisorption with asymmetric bonds, and case 3: physisorption with symmetric bonds. These three cases of CeO2 binding are present on Au(001) and Au(110), but only cases 2 and 3 occur on Au(111).

items.title: A Framework for Closed-Loop Robotic Assembly, Alignment and Self-Recovery of Precision Optical Systems
items.summary: Robotic automation has transformed scientific workflows in domains such as chemistry and materials science, yet free-space optics, which is a high-precision domain, remains largely manual. Optical systems impose strict spatial and angular tolerances, and their performance is governed by tightly coupled physical parameters, making generalizable automation particularly challenging. In this work, we present a robotics framework for the autonomous construction, alignment, and maintenance of precision optical systems. Our approach integrates a hierarchical computer vision system, optimization routines, and custom-built tools to achieve this functionality. As a representative demonstration, we perform the fully autonomous construction of a tabletop laser cavity from randomly distributed components. The system performs several tasks such as laser beam centering, spatial alignment of multiple beams, resonator alignment, laser mode selection, and self-recovery from induced misalignment and disturbances. By achieving closed-loop autonomy for highly sensitive optical systems, this work establishes a foundation for autonomous optical experiments for applications across scientific domains.

items.title: Do Not Let the Prior Heal the Anomaly: Selective Anchoring for Detection from Incomplete Measurements
items.summary: Generative priors can recover anatomical detail from incomplete medical measurements, but may erase the very lesions that imaging aims to detect, even when the measurements contain evidence of them. We introduce selective anchoring that protects reliably measured image components from prior-driven changes, while allowing expressive generative models to reconstruct unresolved structure. Acquisition uncertainty in the protected components is either added deterministically to the downstream test or carried by the ensemble through stochastic perturbations of the readings. We implement this principle as a wrapper for pretrained diffusion and flow samplers and as AnchoredFM, a fast constrained flow model. Under a linear-Gaussian measurement model, the protected coefficients are unbiased in expectation and achieve nominal interval coverage across repeated acquisitions, independently of the learned prior. Across sparse-view CT, accelerated brain MRI, and photoacoustic tomography, selective anchoring improves lesion contrast preservation and uncertainty reliability, and can reduce reconstruction error within lesions. For tumor detection in accelerated MRI, with a healthy reference estimated from the measurements alone, deterministic anchoring raises mean AUROC across eight samplers from 78.4% to 84.6% and lesion sensitivity at 0.25 false-positive marks per slice from 38.8% to 47.5%, with gains in all four predefined tumor-size groups. At thresholds frozen on healthy validation data, mean sensitivity rises from 20.2% to 44.1% (37.6% with stochastic anchoring). These findings show how expressive generative priors can reconstruct unresolved anatomy without healing away the abnormalities that the measurements support.

items.title: Functional classification of metabolic networks
items.summary: Chemical reaction networks underpin biological and physical phenomena across scales, from microbial interactions to planetary atmosphere dynamics. Bacterial communities exhibit complex competitive interactions for resources, human organs and tissues demonstrate specialized biochemical functions, and planetary atmospheres can display diverse organic and inorganic chemical processes. Despite their complexity, comparing these networks remains a challenge due to the vast degrees of freedom shaped, respectively, by evolution, cell differentiation, and planetary formation. In biological systems, comparative genomics has been pivotal in tracing evolutionary trajectories and classifying organisms via DNA sequences. However, purely genomic classifications often fail to capture functional roles within ecological systems. Metabolic changes driven by nutrient availability highlight the need for classification schemes that integrate metabolic information. Here we introduce a computational framework for comparing chemical reaction networks by measuring distances between the nullspaces of their stoichiometric matrices, corresponding to the spaces of unconstrained steady-state fluxes and conservation laws. Applying this framework to human gut microbiome data shows that nullspace geometry captures organization that is not reducible to phylogenetic relatedness or network-overlap. External phenotype prediction shows that stoichiometric nullspace geometry provides phenotype-specific information complementary to competing descriptors, with phenotype-specific advantages that persist when complete genera are withheld. The generalizability of metabolic Grassmann distances is illustrated by application to chemical reaction networks in human tissue and planetary atmospheres, highlighting its potential for developing functional comparisons from geometric descriptors across diverse chemical reaction systems.

items.title: Quantization concealment of angular momentum: dynamic origin of spins
items.summary: Since their introduction, spins of elementary particles remain a phenomenological addition to modern quantum theories. While relatively recent studies on Dirac and other linearized equations of motion have revealed the spatial current nature of the spin magnetic moment (instead of the commonly pictured self-rotation), the dynamical origin of this circulating current remains unresolved. Here, we expose a long-overlooked generic shortcoming of wave mechanics ("quantization concealment of angular momentum") that undesirably reduces the canonical angular momentum of bound eigen-modes and renders incomplete the minimal coupling to magnetic fields. Recovering the kinetic orbital angular momentum resolves $1s$-orbital's counterintuitive "zero" angular momentum and reproduces all planar modes' anomalous Zeeman splitting. Regarding spins as effective remedy to the concealment offers natural explanations to their main puzzles: 1) dynamical origin of spin magnetic moment and 2) frame invariance of spin angular momentum. This implies absence of spin magnetic moment for free particles, a strong prediction verifiable through Stern-Gerlach experiments on electrons.

items.title: Parametric neural-network wavefunctions across a bosonic phase transition
items.summary: We propose Boseformer, a universal attention-based neural-network architecture for representing the wavefunctions of particles with bosonic quantum statistics, including superfluid and crystal phases. The model is trained to generate the wavefunction as a function of a Hamiltonian parameter across the quantum phase transition between these phases. Once trained with variational Monte Carlo optimization, it can serve as a foundation model describing the phase transition without the need to retrain it for individual parameter values. We demonstrate our method on a system of two-dimensional bosons with $1/r^3$ repulsive interaction.

items.title: The Contrast Order: An Order-Based Image Quality Criterion for Nonlinear Beamformers
items.summary: Many modern ultrasound beamformers report improved image quality when evaluated using classical criteria like the contrast ratio and contrast-to-noise ratio, which are based on summary statistics of regions of interest (ROIs). However, nonlinear beamformers and post-processing methods can substantially alter these statistics, raising concerns that the reported improvements may reflect changes in dynamic range or remapping rather than a reflection of true information gain, such as clutter suppression. Introduced recently, the generalized contrast-to-noise ratio (gCNR) is designed to address these concerns, but it requires implementation-dependent density estimation. We propose herein a new, simpler, image quality criterion, called the contrast order (CO), defined as the expected value of the sign of the difference in brightness between two ROIs. The CO is invariant under all strictly monotonic transformations of the image values, as it depends only on their relative ordering, and is interpretable as the probability that one ROI is brighter than the other minus the probability that it is darker. Unlike the gCNR, the CO has a simple unbiased estimator whose variance provably decreases with the number of samples in each ROI. We further propose the effective contrast ratio (ECR), which calibrates the contrast order to the familiar contrast ratio such that the two coincide under ideal Rayleigh-speckle statistics. Together, the CO and ECR provide order- and sign-preserving, dynamic-range-invariant criteria for evaluating lesion contrast, offering a principled alternative to classical and newer image quality criteria when assessing modern beamformers.

items.title: A multiscale composition method for tracking electron bunches from periodically nanostructured photocathodes
items.summary: Nanoholes and other periodic structures on a photocathode can enhance emission by increasing optical absorption and concentrating light. The curvature of a nanohole also alters electron emission directions and the local accelerating field. For the injector considered here, resolving holes of 200 nm nominal width across a laser spot 0.87 mm in diameter is computationally not feasible. We propose a multiscale composition method for tracking electron bunches from nanostructured photocathodes through rf injectors using conventional beam dynamics codes. For a cathode patterned with a 41x41 array of nanoholes, the method reproduces the transverse phase space obtained by resolving every hole in WarpX. The projected emittances agree to within 0.1% in both planes. We then apply this method to calculate the dynamics of a 100 pC bunch in an rf photoinjector with solenoid focusing. For a flat cathode with smooth emission across the same laser spot, the central-slice emittances at 5 m are about 15% above the nominal thermal emittance. The predicted central-slice emittances for the nanostructured cathode exceed those for the flat cathode by 13% horizontally and 19% vertically. The vertical emittance in this slice is modestly larger than the horizontal. No periodic modulation is visible in the transverse phase-space projections of the whole bunch.

items.title: Self-arresting vortex rearrangements in pinned spinning-down superfluids
items.summary: Superfluids, in a spinning-down container with pinning centres, exhibit sudden collective migration of quantized vortices. The onset, progress, and termination of this process remain poorly understood. Here, we show that: 1) the first exodus of vortices occurs when a sector of the vortex array, having a minimum opening angle, is vacated close to the wall; 2) driven by this exodus, the superfluid flow near the boundary continually decreases in strength and arrests the exit; and 3) the resultant depletion region has well-defined dimensions---governed primarily by the critical unpinning velocity, the container size, and the initial rotation rate---that limit the angular momentum transferred to the container. We conclude by discussing the relevance to pulsar glitches.

items.title: Dissipative quadratic soliton mode-locked optical parametric oscillator
items.summary: Femtosecond mode-locked lasers are foundational to ultrafast science, yet their spectral reach remains constrained by the finite emission bandwidth of available gain media. Optical parametric oscillators (OPOs) overcome this constraint but typically require complex synchronous pumping by external femtosecond lasers. Here we demonstrate a fundamentally different approach: passive mode-locking of a continuous-wave-driven, doubly resonant degenerate OPO via the spontaneous formation of femtosecond dissipative quadratic solitons (DQS). We show that phase-matched intracavity cascaded quadratic nonlinearity (PICQN), enabled by negligible pump-signal walk-off in a doubly resonant cavity, generates a non-local effective Kerr nonlinearity (EKN) that governs the cavity dynamics and drives soliton formation. The engineered EKN exceeds the intrinsic material Kerr nonlinearity by more than three orders of magnitude and is continuously tunable in magnitude and sign via pump phase detuning, enabling a paradigm shift from dispersion to nonlinearity engineering for dissipative soliton formation. Comprehensive stability analysis reveals distinct dynamical regimes governed by pumping and cavity conditions, providing a versatile framework for exploring previously understudied quadratic soliton physics. Experimentally, we observe bichromatic femtosecond DQSs at 1572 nm and 786 nm with pulse durations of 336 fs and 447 fs, respectively, peak powers up to 150 W, and a conversion efficiency of 5% under 600 mW continuous-wave pumping. Our work establishes a simple, flexible, and scalable architecture for femtosecond OPOs that bypasses the need for synchronized mode-locked pump lasers. By shifting from traditional dispersion engineering to in-situ nonlinearity engineering, this platform extends the reach of soliton-based technologies and enables dissipative solitons across diverse platforms and spectral regimes.

items.title: Certificate-Based Verification of Pulsed Field Ablation Models
items.summary: Computational models of cardiac pulsed field ablation predict the lesion as the tissue where the electric field exceeds a lethal threshold. Their numerical error is rarely bounded, and automated pipelines increasingly run them without an expert checking each result. To verify each run, we separate the question "was the stated model solved correctly?" from the solver that answers it. An untrusted solver returns its answer with a certificate, which consists of a potential with the correct electrode and ground values and an exactly charge-conserving current. A small independent checker verifies the certificate against a written specification of the physics. Using the Prager-Synge hypercircle theorem evaluated in ball arithmetic, it turns the certificate into guaranteed two-sided bounds on the impedance and on the root-mean-square field of every tile of a lesion map, also over a range of blood/tissue conductivity ratios. The bounds cover numerical error only; whether the model describes tissue is a question of validation. A vectorized version of the checker takes about a tenth of our solver's time. For a focal electrode in contact, the tile-resolved depth at 1000 V and 700 V/cm is proven to lie in 3.50-3.75 mm for every ratio from 1.7 to 3.75. For a bipolar catheter, certified depths overlap published in-vivo depths. Where they differ from a published reference model, the certificates prove that the difference is not our numerical error. We compare the certificate with a grid convergence study on the same solver. On graded grids, the study is sharper for local fields but remains an estimate. On uniform grids, it fails to converge at the electrode edge, where the certificate still gives a valid bracket. Solvers that deliberately solve equations other than the specified ones pass the grid convergence study, but the certificates refute the impedances they report or leave them unsupported.

items.title: Source Detection in Complex Networks: Observability, Identifiability, and Inference Frameworks
items.summary: Tracing diffusion to its origin is a central inverse problem in complex networks, with applications ranging from epidemic investigation and information spreading to cyber incidents and disruptions in interconnected systems. Although source-detection methods have advanced along diverse methodological lines, their capabilities cannot be assessed independently of the evidence on which they operate. Network structure and diffusion dynamics determine which propagation histories are possible, while the observation mechanism determines which traces of those histories are retained. This review develops an information-centric and identifiability-aware perspective that connects these elements to source inference. We organize existing research around three overlapping observation settings: complete state snapshots, incomplete or noisy observations, and sensor-based observation and design. Within this organization, we examine structural, probabilistic, message-passing, simulation-based, and learning-based methods, comparing their required inputs, underlying assumptions, inference mechanisms, and computational demands. System-theoretic observability, statistical identifiability, and information-theoretic constraints provide complementary ways to examine what the available observations can reveal, while separating limitations of the evidence from those of estimation. Drawing on applications across epidemiological, information, biological, neural, and socioeconomic systems, we identify challenges in uncertainty assessment, model robustness, transfer across networks, and the acquisition of informative observations. This synthesis clarifies the conditions under which diffusion sources can be identified and how inference methods should be selected according to the available observations.

items.title: Nonlinear non-modal stability and minimal perturbations in electroconvection driven by unipolar injection
items.summary: Electroconvection in a dielectric liquid subjected to unipolar charge injection is subcritical. Convection can be sustained well below the threshold of linear stability theory, and experiments report onset far below it. We use nonlinear non-modal optimization to determine the smallest charge perturbations that trigger convection below the linear threshold. The method, based on a direct--adjoint formulation of the full electrohydrodynamic equations, recovers the classical linear threshold in the limit of small amplitudes. At finite amplitude, the most dangerous perturbations are localized charge deficits rather than excesses, because a deficit relaxes more slowly under Coulomb repulsion. The minimal perturbation needed for transition grows from about 0.5% of the injected charge near the linear threshold to 3% at two thirds of it, where the convective branch ends, in agreement with direct numerical simulations. Near the critical amplitude, trajectories approach an unstable steady state, the edge state, that separates the basins of attraction of rest and convection and originates from the critical linear mode. The damped oscillatory modes involved in the growth of the optimal perturbations are transit-time modes of the ion drift. The convective mode is the first of them, made stationary by the coupling with the flow, which explains why the instability sets in as a steady motion. Small charge fluctuations can therefore lower the onset of electroconvection to about two thirds of the linear threshold, helping to explain the discrepancy between linear theory and experiments.

items.title: An Implicit Compact-Kernel Material Point Method for Computational Solid Mechanics
items.summary: The numerical performance of the material point method (MPM) is strongly governed by the particle-grid kernel, which controls the trade-off among smoothness, locality, numerical diffusion, contact accuracy, and computational cost. Although wide-support smooth kernels can effectively suppress cell-crossing instability, they often introduce increased numerical diffusion, artificial contact gaps, and higher transfer cost. In contrast, the suitability of compact-kernel designs for implicit computational solid mechanics remains unclear. In this work, we develop an implicit formulation of the Compact-Kernel Material Point Method (CK-MPM) building on the framework of Liu et al. [2025], and assess its performance through benchmark problems in linear and nonlinear solid mechanics. Numerical assessment comprises cantilever bending, Hertzian contact, narrow-clearance free fall, and colliding hyperelastic rings, supplemented by a transfer-only diffusion test and spatial and temporal refinement studies. Implicit CK-MPM mitigates the cell-crossing stress noise and numerical energy loss observed in linear MPM, while retaining bending and energy responses comparable to those of quadratic B-spline MPM. Meanwhile, its more localized transfers improve contact-pressure accuracy and reduce the artificial contact gaps and early-contact artifacts associated with the wider-support quadratic kernel. These results demonstrate that the developed implicit formulation retains CK-MPM's favorable balance between smoothness and transfer locality in static and dynamic solid-mechanics analysis.

items.title: Cell and nuclear shapes predict confined motility
items.summary: Cancer metastasis relies on an enhanced property of cells to migrate efficiently even through constrictions smaller than their nucleus. Both cell and nuclear morphology may influence this process. How these morphologies relate to the likelihood that a cell will transit through a constriction remains unclear. Here we combine microfluidic experiments with machine learning to predict whether MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells are able to transit through narrow constrictions. Cells migrate within vertically confined boxes, and may migrate into neighboring boxes by transiting through constrictions, requiring a deformation of the nucleus. Defining a set of 12 geometrical features derived from cell and nuclear contours, we find that their average values are not statistically indicative of whether or not a cell will transit. To overcome this limitation, we use trajectories to train classifiers and evaluate their ability to predict future transit events. We find that the cell area and cell circularity carry most of the predictive information and less circular cells are more likely to transit. Without retraining, the models also predict transit through narrower constrictions and in more adhesive substrates. Morphological features of cells about 30 minutes before a transit event proved most informative about future transit events occurring or not. Together, our results show that cell shape, readable from simple contour descriptors, contains a transferable but condition-dependent signature of imminent transit.

items.title: Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train Spectral Solver for High-Resolution PDEs with Non-Periodic Boundary Conditions
items.summary: Tensor train (TT) methods enable high-resolution computational mechanics simulations by exploiting low-rank structure in discretized fields and operators. While the superfast Fourier transform (SFFT) has enabled efficient TT-based spectral solvers for periodic problems, corresponding representations for non-periodic boundary conditions remain underexplored. We introduce the superfast cosine and sine transforms (SFCT and SFST), extending the TT spectral framework to homogeneous Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, respectively. Building on a quantum-circuit construction of the discrete cosine and sine transforms, we derive both transforms from a shared TT operator representation and prove that their TT ranks are bounded by $6r_S$, independently of the discretization order, where $r_S$ is the rank of the SFFT at the prescribed accuracy. The measured ranks plateau near 32 for grid sizes up to $2^{26}$ points. For Rayleigh-Bénard convection, spectral pressure projection achieves up to a 7-fold speedup in the Poisson solve relative to a preconditioned physical-space TT solver while maintaining comparable accuracy. Three-dimensional computational homogenization achieves a 2-6-fold speedup and a 4-7-fold reduction in memory consumption compared with the existing TT-based approach. The results establish an efficient TT framework for spectral PDE solvers with non-periodic boundary conditions.

items.title: Fast and Accurate Boys Function Evaluation Using Nonuniform Gridded Taylor Expansions
items.summary: Efficient Boys function evaluation is important for Gaussian integral calculations on both central processing units (CPUs) and graphics processing units (GPUs). Gridded Taylor expansion provides a simple evaluation procedure, but a uniformly spaced reference table requires substantial storage over a wide argument range. We address this limitation using a nonuniform grid whose spacing increases with the argument. For large arguments, we introduce a normalized auxiliary function whose scaling and derivative properties allow it to be evaluated using the same Taylor procedure as the main-domain Boys functions. The main-domain and large-argument reference tables are constructed jointly, with polynomial degrees and grid parameters selected under accuracy and storage constraints. Low-part corrections to the reference values are included to improve the accuracy of the Taylor evaluation. The resulting method is implemented in the Fast and Accurate BOys (FABO) library and evaluated in QUICK and NWChem-Simint. FABO gives the smallest maximum and mean errors among the tested implementations for all three reported error measures, with the largest sampled error being approximately 1.067 units in the last place (ULPs). In application benchmarks, FABO reduces the Fock-build time relative to the original Boys evaluators in both applications and is competitive with the other tested implementations.

items.title: Adding Temperature to the Adiabatic Connection: Hybrid Functionals for Static and Dynamic Correlation
items.summary: Capturing static and dynamic electron correlation simultaneously at manageable computational cost remains a key challenge in electronic structure theory. Motivated by the recurring role of effective temperature in self-consistent field methods we extend the adiabatic connection mechanism from density functional theory (DFT) to include a temperature dimension. The formalism unifies established hybrid functionals with information-density matrix functional theory (i-DMFT) and thermally-assisted-occupation DFT, clarifying their theoretical basis and the respective prescriptions for the temperature parameter. It further gives rise to thermally enhanced hybrid functionals, in which static correlation is captured via fractional occupations generated by an effective "correlation temperature" within thermal Hartree-Fock, while dynamic correlation is described by established density functional approximations. We assess the performance of several thermally enhanced hybrids for different cases where i-DMFT was previously shown to fail. Furthermore, we discuss and test different schemes for determining the correlation temperature and investigate the accuracy of different such choices for a benchmark set of different organic molecules. The results clarify the achievable balance of accuracy, generality, and efficiency, establishing thermally enhanced hybrids as a systematic route toward low-cost treatment of both correlation types.

items.title: Photon number correlations in harmonics driven with classical and quantum light
items.summary: Recent reports of nonclassical intensity correlations in harmonic generation raised questions about whether strong harmonic correlations necessarily imply genuinely quantum behaviour. Here, we compare the low-photon-number perturbative harmonic generation driven by classical and bright squeezed vacuum sources. The latter generates strong auto- and cross-correlations in the harmonic spectrum. Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and heralding measurements show that the cross-correlations are fully classical and can be explained by the common fluctuations from the driving field. A visible scaling of the measured correlation function with mean harmonic flux is observed, which is well-explained by a click detector-response model.

items.title: Integrated lasing and dual-band gain in neodymium-implanted silicon nitride
items.summary: Lasers at wavelengths near 1 micrometer are used in quantum technologies, precision metrology, and sensing. Rare-earth gain at these wavelengths in photonic integrated circuits can reduce the size and enable the scalable fabrication of these lasers. We fabricate neodymium-based integrated waveguide amplifiers and a ring laser using neodymium-implanted LPCVD silicon nitride. The photonic integrated circuits were fabricated on a 200 mm commercial wafer platform, and individual dies were implanted with neodymium ions. We show that the amplifiers provide gain in two bands around wavelengths of 920 nm and 1100 nm, and we show lasing in a ring resonator. This demonstrates that neodymium-implanted LPCVD silicon nitride is a suitable gain material for integrated lasers.

items.title: Whistler instability driven by electron trapping in magnetic dips
items.summary: Using fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations, we show how free energy released by an ion-scale instability reaches electron scales through its effect on the electron distribution. An initial ion temperature anisotropy drives partly compressional ion cyclotron waves, which form magnetic dips. Electrons trapped in these dips develop an enhanced temperature anisotropy and butterfly-shaped distributions, similar to those observed by spacecraft in the Earth's magnetosheath. By tracking the energy transfer in velocity space, we show that the gradients created by trapping drive whistler waves through cyclotron resonance. The whistlers in turn scatter the electrons in pitch angle, flattening velocity-space gradients and heating the electrons along the magnetic field. As a result, the electron anisotropy drops to about half of the double-adiabatic prediction once the whistler power peaks. Our results show that it is the shape of the electron distribution in magnetic dips, rather than its temperature anisotropy alone, that drives the whistlers.

items.title: From Fermions to Vortices: Microscopic Simulations of Phase Ordering in a d-Wave Superconductor
items.summary: Describing bath-induced superconducting phase ordering directly from a microscopic fermionic Hamiltonian remains a formidable challenge. Here we develop a microscopic framework for this problem using the recently introduced adiabatic variational principle (AVP) and demonstrate its application to a two-dimensional $d$-wave superconductor. The central construction maps evolving, spatially inhomogeneous bond-pairing fields onto constrained Bogoliubov-de Gennes states, with the associated Lagrange multipliers determining the thermodynamic driving forces. This enables dissipative evolution of the superconducting order while retaining its microscopic electronic structure, without assuming a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau free-energy functional. Starting from disordered pairing configurations, we resolve the emergence of phase coherence through vortex-antivortex annihilation and the accompanying evolution of local electronic spectra. Vortex decay and dynamical scaling recover the characteristic kinetics of two-dimensional phase ordering, providing a nontrivial benchmark of the framework. The solver-independent AVP formulation opens a route to microscopic studies of dissipative ordering and metastability in superconductors with intertwined stripe and pair-density-wave orders.

items.title: Spatial exceptional points induced by hyperbolicity in an electrostatic spherical shell
items.summary: Exceptional points (EPs) in optics are usually associated with gain and loss or non-reciprocity. In this work we show that a shell with spherical anisotropy supports "spatial EPs" without either. The radial electrostatic problem maps onto a damped oscillator in which the dielectric anisotropy $\varepsilon_r/\varepsilon_t$ is the control parameter. At the EP, the two power-law solutions coalesce spatially and a second, logarithmic solution emerges. Beyond this threshold, the field switches from monotonic decay to spatial oscillation, enabling multiple Fabry-Perot-like resonances. This work reveals how spatial exceptional points modify the optical response of hyperbolic core-shell particles.

items.title: P-ONE-1: the first detector line of the Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment
items.summary: Neutrino telescopes instrument optically transparent media with three-dimensional arrays of photosensors to detect Cherenkov radiation induced by neutrino interactions within or near the instrumented volume. The small cross-sections of the weak interaction and the low neutrino fluxes above TeV energies require vast detector volumes, which only natural media on Earth can realistically provide. Spurred by the detection of the first neutrino sources by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a new generation of neutrino telescopes is emerging to increase the global instrumented volume and detection sensitivity. The Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE) aims to install such a telescope in the Northeast Pacific Ocean, building on established neutrino telescope design targets in collaboration with Ocean Networks Canada (ONC). This article presents the design, integration, and testing of the first P-ONE line, P-ONE-1, in preparation for its deployment and integration into ONC's deep-sea observatory NEPTUNE. Alongside the detector design and integration methods, we detail in-air and in-water system-level validation performed at several test sites in Canada, culminating in the successful construction of P-ONE-1 and its preparation for deployment.

items.title: Cavitation near the oscillating piezoelectric plate in water
items.summary: Gas and vapor bubbles at a wall can reduce the skin friction of a liquid flow. We estimate whether an oscillating piezoelectric plate mounted flush with the wall can create such a near-wall bubble layer by acoustic cavitation. Once the cavitation threshold is reached, the liquid can no longer follow the receding plate, and the excess plate displacement is accommodated by cavitation bubbles forming at the wall; this kinematic argument gives the bubble volume generated per stroke and its energy cost. Homogeneous cavitation in pure water (about -30 MPa) requires pressure amplitudes far beyond those of flat piezoelectric plates and produces submicron bubbles that collapse within nanoseconds. Heterogeneous cavitation on wall and gas nuclei (-0.1 to -1 MPa) is within reach of piezoceramics and concentrates the void on fewer, larger wal-attached bubbles, which survive between strokes if they exceed a few micrometres at 5 MHz. The acoustic power needed to sustain a bubble layer in a turbulent boundary layer at 10 m/s is about 20 kW/m2 for heterogeneous and about 0.4 MW/m2 for homogeneous cavitation.

items.title: Path-probability gradients for optimizing force fields against dynamical observables
items.summary: Machine learning force fields inherit the errors of the electronic-structure methods used to generate their training data, and refining them against experimental measurements provides a direct route beyond this limit. However, such refinement remains difficult for dynamical observables because differentiating chaotic molecular trajectories yields unstable gradients. Here, we introduce PathGrad, which differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of the trajectories themselves. The resulting gradient estimator is accumulated on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives, and its variance remains stable as the trajectory length increases. We validated the gradient estimator against finite-difference calculations and used it to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients together with structural constraints. For water, jointly optimizing diffusion and the oxygen-oxygen radial distribution function also improves the predictions of shear viscosity and rotational relaxation, neither of which is included in the optimization objective. Alignment at a single temperature also improves the apparent activation energies of multiple dynamical observables, bringing their temperature dependences closer to experiments. Moreover, the optimized potential exhibits smaller force errors relative to an independent, higher-level quantum-chemical reference, indicating that alignment with experiments improves the fidelity of the potential energy surface beyond the fitted targets. PathGrad thus establishes a general framework for incorporating experimental observables directly into force field optimizations.

items.title: Geometry and topology of DNA defects
items.summary: DNA defects arise frequently, either as a result of damage, protein binding or the action of molecular enzymes such as an RNA polymerase. Here we combine geometry, atomistic simulations and an analysis of real DNA structures to provide a quantitative characterisation of DNA defects and their dynamics. The composite order parameter describing defects geometrically is a backbone-to-base polar vector, together with a quaternion capturing 3D base orientation in a single strand. There are three types of defects: flips of the polar vector, stacking defects of bases, and composite defects encompassing both. All types of defects feature in realistic structures for DNA and have functional relevance. Additionally, biased molecular dynamics simulations of DNA with an imposed elastic deformation form flip or stacking defects whose abundance and dynamics strongly depend on sequence and type of deformation. Our results provide a link between geometry and biochemistry, and could also be applied, for instance, to identify defects in RNA molecules and nucleosome arrays.

items.title: A unified perspective on wavelength selection for molecular composition inference from diffuse spectroscopy
items.summary: Optical monitoring of living tissue targeting quantification of molecular composition is an active area of research. In the case of broadband spectroscopy, one can attempt to extract molecular, or more precisely, chromophore concentration from a broad-range spectrum of the reflected light. However, selecting the shortest wavelength range sufficient for quantitative optical monitoring remains an open problem. Various wavelength optimization methods are scattered throughout the literature, however, there is no unified view to date. Our work's motivation is to construct a wavelength selection framework by unifying existing selection approaches and propose a novel projection-based method that allows for the pre-identification of a wavelength range that is adequate for the final selection. The framework specifically focuses on proposing different methods that quantify match or mismatch between the chosen light-matter interaction model, defined by the chosen endmembers (e.g. molecular chromophores), and the measured intensity from the spectroscopic data. To evaluate the framework, we perform a retrospective analysis on a broadband spectroscopy dataset of piglets during an induced hypoxia-ischemia state. Overall, we show that our novel projection-based method can be used for band selection, and that existing approaches can be used in conjunction to select an optimal minimal wavelength set that satisfies biophysical model constraints.

items.title: Recipe for near-unity efficient frequency conversion via transient molecular modulation
items.summary: Frequency transduction technologies are an essential element for interfacing devices operating at distinct spectral regions. Specifically, the conversion of weak signals between different wavelengths is a fundamental requirement of quantum networks, where conversion efficiency is critical for preserving the statistical properties of light. In this regard, molecular modulation in gas-filled hollow-core fibers offers a promising approach for highly-tunable linear frequency conversion of classical and quantum light. However, recent experimental studies in this subject have struggled to overcome a saturation in conversion efficiency to about 70%, which, although high, might impair the faithful transfer of quantum properties upon conversion. In this work, we discuss a route to surpass this limitation that identifies the key factors to consider for obtaining quantum efficiencies exceeding 99%. These results might pave the way to viable fiber-based quantum transduction schemes for next-generation quantum networks.

items.title: Determining the electron-hole pair creation energy in a 4H-SiC p-n diode via X-ray spectroscopy
items.summary: This paper reports on a measurement to determine the electron-hole pair creation energy in a 4H-SiC p-n diode. By measuring the spectra of several X-ray sources and comparing the response between the silicon-carbide diode and a commercial silicon diode, the electron-hole pair creation energy in 4H-SiC is determined to be (7.87 $\pm$ 0.09) eV. This is the first result obtained using X-ray spectra from several sources and including an estimate of the uncertainty. The result is in good agreement with studies of comparable devices.

items.title: Packing the Bragg sphere: complete three-dimensional photonic band gaps at the refractive index of polymers (1.55)
items.summary: Complete 3D photonic band gaps have so far been found only at refractive-index contrasts of about 1.9 and above, reached by rod-connected diamond lattice structures. Reciprocal-space design of quasiperiodic structures recently achieved considerable emission attenuation at much lower contrasts [L. Maiwald et al., Adv. Optical Mater. 10, 2100785 (2022)]. Here we implement systematic search and reciprocal-space design of periodic 3D structures with complete band gaps, solving a discrete optimization problem on an integer lattice. A gap above a high band needs the strongest Fourier components of the dielectric close to the Bragg sphere of that band. Crystals with large cells, started from Fourier peaks at the vertices of a polyhedron on this sphere and optimized against densely refined band edges, open complete gaps down to an index contrast of 1.55, that of common polymers against air. A rational approximant of an icosidodecahedron gave the most efficient location of the Fourier peaks among the polyhedra tested. Numerical calculations confirm the gaps over a resolution series, with band edges searched over the whole Brillouin zone. The best designs are connected porous networks, suited to a microwave test with printed polymer. A rigorous bound, valid for any structure, does not exclude gaps at lower index, and the next rational approximants of the icosidodecahedron, whose Bragg zones match bands 576 and 2440 almost exactly, point to where gaps at even lower contrast may be sought.

items.title: Recovery of Extended Modes from the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect Due to Local Nonlinearity on a Boundary
items.summary: Localization in continuum spectra known as the non-Hermitian skin effect is widely believed to be a consequence of nontrivial topology of bulk bands. However, the robustness of the non-Hermitian skin effect against nonlinear effects is still a nontrivial problem. We here reveal that single-bond nonlinearity on a boundary can recover extended modes in a non-Hermitian tight-binding model. We propose and analyze a one-dimensional minimal model, where we introduce a nonlinear phase shift of a hopping term only at boundary sites. We also propose a possible photonic setup to dynamically observe the nonlinearity-induced extended modes as a steady state. Our results thus challenge the conventional notion of the non-Hermitian skin effect by revealing its dependence on nonlinear boundary conditions.

items.title: Squeezed states of light after high-harmonic generation in excited atomic systems
items.summary: High-harmonic generation (HHG) has recently emerged as a promising method for generating non-classical states of light with frequencies spanning from the infrared up to the extreme ultraviolet regime. In this work, we theoretically investigate the generation of squeezed states of light through HHG processes in atomic systems that had been initially driven to their first excited state. Our study reveals significant single-mode squeezing in both the driving field and low-order harmonic modes. Additionally, we characterize two-mode squeezing features in the generated states, both between fundamental and harmonic modes, and among the harmonic modes themselves. Using these correlations, we demonstrate the generation of optical Schrödinger kitten states through heralding measurements, specifically via photon subtraction in one of the modes influenced by two-mode squeezing.

items.title: Micrometer-sized magnonic three-port rectilinear circulator
items.summary: The development of miniaturized non-reciprocal microwave technologies compatible with integrated circuit architectures remains a critical challenge for modern information technology. Here, we present the first experimental characterization of a micron-sized prototypical magnon circulator. Taking advantage of the chiral excitation of spin-waves via nanowire gratings, we propose an original design of a circulator involving three channels of rectilinear and unidirectional spin-wave beams. We demonstrate via a full 3-port spin-wave spectroscopy a genuine spin-wave circulation between the three ports. The narrow frequency band of operation can be tuned over a broad range of frequencies (2-8 GHz) with both an external field of up to 100 mT, and the dimensions of the grating specifying the wavevectors. This proposed scheme opens up possibilities for architectures of integrated and miniaturized non-reciprocal microwave devices.

items.title: Programmable multipartite entanglement analogues
items.summary: Quantum entanglement underpins the quantum information science. Its multipartite forms distribute coherence across several subsystems, but controlling their composition and order is increasingly difficult as more subsystems participate. Classical nonseparable waves provide accessible analogues of these structures, although existing implementations largely fix the participating degrees of freedom through their generating architectures. Here we overcome this constraint by making multipartiteness itself programmable in electromagnetic fields. A spatiotemporal metasurface reconfigures the identity and number of coherently linked state spaces independently across polarization, frequency, orbital angular momentum, wavevector direction, and orthogonal envelope modes. We realize complete Bell-like and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger-like families from bipartite to five-partite order and exchange constituents at fixed order. To our knowledge, the five-partite state has the highest multipartite order experimentally realized in classical electromagnetic fields. These results establish the distribution of coherence across physical state spaces as a programmable property of classical waves and provide a platform for studying selected structures of multipartite quantum states without invoking quantum entanglement or nonlocality.

items.title: Heat Reduction in Erbium-Doped Microresonator
items.summary: We investigate anti-Stokes fluorescence in a 106-micrometer-diameter silica whispering-gallery-mode microresonator coated with erbium-doped sol-gel, assessing its potential for reduced optical heating. Near-infrared fluorescence spectra acquired under pulsed excitation near 1.55 micrometers exhibit a mean emitted photon energy above the pump photon energy. Measurements over a temperature range of 25 to 62 degrees Celsius show that the mean fluorescence photon energy increases with externally controlled temperature. The measured pump-wavelength dependence is consistent with an absorption-weighted spectral model, which predicts an optimum near 1562.65 nm for the investigated spectral figure of merit. Resonance-dependent emission patterns further motivate a dual-frequency pumping scheme using two higher-order whispering-gallery modes. Calculated time-averaged field profiles indicate that complementary modal distributions can provide more uniform excitation near the equator. These results characterize spectral conditions relevant to fluorescence-based heat reduction and suggest a route toward improved spatial pump coverage. Demonstrating net optical refrigeration requires additional measurements of absorbed pump power and an independent thermal readout.

items.title: Why wait? Optimal rules for intertemporal decisions across life history, economics and machine learning
items.summary: When should we take a smaller reward now rather than wait for a larger one later? This question recurs across evolutionary biology, behavioral ecology, psychology, economics and artificial intelligence, yet each field treats temporal discounting differently. We show that intertemporal decisions across these disciplines share a common structure and a single optimal rule: wait while the growth rate of the reward exceeds the discount rate, and act when the two rates become equal. For a single decision, this rule defines an optimal waiting time; for a continuous reward stream, it becomes an equation of motion for quantities apportioned over time, such as consumption or fertility. We derive reward and discount rates from explicit mechanisms, including mortality and other hazards, uncertainty and risk aversion, population growth, capital depreciation, dread, subsistence thresholds and the value of information, with examples from laboratory choice, retirement, maturation, resource extraction, capital accumulation and exploration. The framework shows how apparent anomalies, including hyperbolic discounting, the sign effect and the impatience of deprivation, can arise from the relative structure of rewards and hazards rather than from fixed preferences. Finally, we identify what must be measured to explain and modify temporal preferences in experiments and policy.

items.title: Neutron Spectroscopy Transformed: Deuterated ZIF-8 and Machine-Learned Potentials Catch Nitrogen Threading Its Gates
items.summary: We report a step change in what inelastic neutron scattering (INS) can reveal, by combining machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with deliberate deuteration of the sample. INS's prowess in charting framework and guest motions within porous materials during in situ dosing has historically had one caveat: costly density-functional-theory calculations are a major bottleneck in the speed and depth of analysis. We show that rapid frontier MLIPs remove this bottleneck on both counts, keeping pace with the experiment while bringing a new level of insight. Deuterating the linkers of ZIF-8 pries apart bands that overlap in the hydrogenous framework, and we test four MLIPs against eight stages of nitrogen dosing at 77 K. On loading, a previously unobserved band appears at 270 cm^-1 and grows gradually through the dosing series. The simulations trace it to single N2 molecules threaded end-on through four-ring windows, each turning its ring of linkers and propping the window open, and unbiased dynamics catch molecules threading into the windows on their own, finding a free-energy trap that crowding stabilizes. This is the first vibrational signature of the threaded state and, crucially, its intensity directly counts the threading over the slow, macroscopic timescale of gas uptake, in situ. More broadly, the simulations explain how each framework band responds to its guests, establishing MLIP-assisted inelastic neutron scattering as a route to mechanism, not just assignment.

items.title: Impact of Taylor-Aris dispersion on chemical patterns in confined channel flows
items.summary: Chemical patterns form through non-linear interactions between different species. We study how confined channel flows affect pattern formation using the Brusselator as a paradigmatic activator-inhibitor model. An invariant-manifold method for slender channels reduces the advection-diffusion-reaction equation to one spatial dimension, with species transported at the mean flow velocity and molecular diffusivities replaced by the classical Taylor-Aris dispersion coefficients. We obtain the phase diagram as a function of the Péclet number (i.e., the relative strength of advection to diffusion), the channel slenderness, and the diffusivity ratio of the species. Our analytical results demonstrate that the classical Turing criterion can become inverted at large Péclet numbers and, thus, channel flow can trigger pattern formation even when the molecular diffusivities violate the classical Turing condition, and conversely destroy pre-existing patterns. Both predictions are confirmed by direct numerical simulations, which show advected stripe patterns, whose wavelength can be predicted by our reduced theory, as well as oscillatory dynamics. These findings highlight that hydrodynamic flows can modify chemical mixing and thereby profoundly affect pattern formation in channel geometries.

items.title: Mixing and Preserving Properties of Non-van der Waals 2D Materials in Sandwich-like Heterostructures
items.summary: Heterostructure interfaces created by stacking two-dimensional (2D) materials outline an appealing route towards achieving advanced electronic and magnetic functionalities at the nanoscale. Non-van der Waals (non-vdW) sandwich-like heterostructures (HSs) are build out of non-vdW 2D materials derived from non-layered crystals and establish a new frontier enabling strong interfacial coupling. Employing ab initio density functional theory (DFT), we investigate two classes of such trilayer HSs: purely non-vdW assemblies and hybrid vdW/non-vdW/vdW stacks. We show that non-vdW sandwiches undergo pronounced geometric reconstruction forming chemically bonded interfaces with large absolute binding energies up to an order of magnitude larger than those of conventional vdW HSs. These strong interactions drive extensive electronic hybridization, band gap renormalization, and tunable interlayer magnetic coupling. In contrast, vdW encapsulation largely protects the intrinsic atomic and electronic structure of the non-vdW sheet from the environment , while enabling charge transfer doping of the vdW layers. Our results thus establish sandwich HSs a versatile interface design platform, spanning interaction regimes from weakly perturbed encapsulation to strongly interacting chemically bonded systems with emergent electronic and magnetic behavior.

items.title: AI-Assisted Topological High-Harmonic Spectroscopy for Characterizing Crystal Symmetries and Nonlinear Responses
items.summary: Structured light has emerged as a unique tool for probing nonlinear light-matter interactions. Particularly interesting is its interaction with anisotropic media, such as crystalline materials, whose anisotropic responses encode information about their electronic properties. Recently, topological high-harmonic spectroscopy was introduced as an all-optical approach to extract the anisotropic nonlinear response of graphene from harmonic spatial intensity profiles. Here, topological high-harmonic spectroscopy is combined with artificial intelligence (AI) to retrieve the anisotropic non-linear response and crystal symmetry of atomically thin materials. A convolutional neural network is trained and validated to learn the inverse mapping between harmonic far-field intensity profiles and the nonlinear response of materials exhibiting different rotational symmetries. Comparisons with microscopic high-harmonic-generation simulations demonstrate the accurate retrieval of distinct effective nonlinear responses in single-symmetry crystals, such as single-layer graphene and bilayer graphene with different stacking orders, and in crystals exhibiting multiple symmetry components, such as monolayer hexagonal boron nitride. Macroscopic high-harmonic-generation simulations assess the robustness and applicability limits of the technique. These results establish AI-assisted topological high-harmonic spectroscopy as a fast, contactless tool for characterizing nonlinear optical responses and crystal symmetries without phase-resolved measurements, opening prospects for applications to complex systems such as polycrystals and van der Waals heterostructures.

items.title: Effect of humidity and phase transition on turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour in atmospheric turbulent flows
items.summary: We investigate the effect of humidity on turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour in atmospheric turbulent flows taking into account the effect of phase transitions on turbulent transport.
