Across three datasets, AMRT generalizes to unseen trials and subjects and demonstrates transfer potential across neural recordings and movement paradigms, highlighting the potential of shared neural representations and anchor-and-refine decoding for generalizable continuous neural control.

items.title: Pharmaco-mechanical computational simulation of atherosclerotic arteries: effects of calcium channel blockers on local stress distributions
items.summary: This paper presents a computational model integrating transmural drug transport, smooth muscle cell contraction, nonlinear anisotropic material behavior, and residual stresses to investigate the effects of calcium channel blockers~(CCBs) on local stress distributions in atherosclerotic arteries. The balance of linear momentum is coupled with a three-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation for the drug transport. Smooth muscle contraction is modeled phenomenologically based on a chemo-mechanical model that incorporates the effects of stretch on intracellular calcium dynamics and calcium sensitization. A novel drug-tissue interaction model is proposed to capture the effects of CCBs on intracellular calcium and thus on smooth muscle contraction. Material parameters are identified by fitting to experimental data from the literature and finite element simulations are conducted on five exemplary atherosclerotic arterial geometries reconstructed from histological cross-sections. Simulation results show that although CCBs reduce the stresses in the media through reduced smooth muscle contraction, they shift load to the fibrous cap, whose stress increases in all five geometries (median of up to 28.9~kPa). This increase varies strongly between plaque morphologies and becomes smaller with lower smooth muscle tone before treatment, lower drug concentrations in the arterial wall and increasing axial pre-stretch. A blood pressure reduction of 10~mmHg already lowers it to a median of at most 3.8~kPa in four of the five geometries. Our findings suggest that CCBs may increase the rupture risk of vulnerable plaques with highly loaded fibrous caps under insufficient blood pressure reduction, which remains to be confirmed experimentally and clinically.

items.title: Ten simple rules for non-visual, reproducible and accessible bioinformatics
items.summary: Bioinformatics workflows rely heavily on visual representations. Quality-control plots, cell embeddings, heatmaps, genome-browser tracks, and interactive dashboards are not merely illustrations, but instruments for making analytical decisions. For blind and low-vision researchers who use screen readers, braille displays, or audio-based interfaces, these create a barrier: the evidence used to justify an analysis is often encoded in visual form, while the underlying decision remains undocumented. We argue that non-visual accessibility and computational reproducibility are closely aligned, as they both require analyses to be transparent and to record why decisions were made. We present ten simple rules for non-visual bioinformatics, covering plots as decision records, cautious use of AI-generated figure descriptions, accessible computing environments, text-first literate programming, structured data and metadata, compact object summaries, accessible publication formats, collaboration practices, shared community infrastructure, and accessibility as part of FAIR research. The intended audience is computational biologists and developers. Using single-cell RNA-seq as a running example, we show that the accessible equivalent of a plot is a structured decision record. That is, a plot companion that goes beyond storing the underlying data by also stating the purpose of the analysis and the resulting quantitative evidence and uncertainty. We argue that treating accessibility in this way makes bioinformatics more inclusive and also more transparent and auditable.

items.title: Open-fMIND: A Large-Scale Open-Access fMRI Corpus for Pretraining Brain Foundation Models
items.summary: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by data use agreements and dominated by a small number of acquisition protocols, while the thousands of openly licensed datasets on OpenNeuro are individually small, heterogeneously organized, and unprocessed. We present the first release of Open-fMIND, a uniformly preprocessed, openly accessible corpus of parcellated fMRI timeseries from 322 OpenNeuro studies, comprising 11,379 subjects and 45,731 functional runs. Each run is preprocessed with fMRIPrep and parcellated under 52 atlases spanning 14 families, yielding a massive 2.4 million timeseries. Timeseries are released either denoised with our default pipeline (preproc) or as the fMRIPrep output with its confound files (quasiraw), with functional connectivity matrices, per-run provenance and motion metadata. Open-fMIND is intended as a pretraining resource for self-supervised brain representation learning. Pretraining on it yields downstream performance comparable to that obtained with UK Biobank.

items.title: Predator-associated cues promote host riding, and coupling to mobile hosts improves survival in an epizoic limpet
items.summary: A host with multiscale movements may be difficult for a small animal to intercept or predict. Boarding turns that moving target into a source of locomotion. The snail Tegula nigerrima previously showed statistical signatures consistent with near-critical locomotor dynamics over limited ranges. We examined how the facultative epizoic limpet Lottia tenuisculpta approaches and boards this host, and whether host mobility improves rider survival. Crab-associated waterborne cues increased riding (19/80 without cues versus 42/76 with cues) and visible host--limpet distance closure. Paired trajectories of eventual riders captured both animals' projected movement toward one another during a nominal ten-minute window ending at the movement-analysis reference frame. Normalised by each animal's shell size, the limpet's projected contribution exceeded the host's in 22/58 pairs. A complementary exploratory assay compared each limpet's cumulative path length on an assigned surface with its no-mucus baseline at a common observation time. Log-transformed ratios varied less among individuals in gastropod-mucus groups than in the no-mucus group. Across the observed frequency range, a matched-trial comparison estimated a 1.21-fold cue-present to cue-absent amplitude ratio (95% recording-date bootstrap interval: 0.97--1.59); the treatment difference in high-frequency spectral slope remained uncertain. Survival was higher on mobile than fixed hosts, with shells occupied in both treatments (posterior median hazard ratio, fixed versus mobile: 2.1). These findings connect the behavioural formation of host--rider coupling to a survival benefit from host mobility, illustrating how one animal gains access to the multiscale locomotion of another.

items.title: Koopman Operator Analysis of EEG Microstate Dynamics Reveals a Cross-Dataset, Hearing-Level Adjusted Signature of Tinnitus
items.summary: While major progress has been made in identifying EEG biomarkers for chronic Tinnitus, hearing loss remains as a major confound that must be accounted for in the identified effect. These markers have rarely been tested across independent datasets, a further test of robustness. We analyzed resting-state EEG microstate statistics, and developed a Koopman-operator description of the same microstate signal, carry a tinnitus-related difference that replicates across sites and survives adjustment for hearing level. Three public resting-state datasets (335 subjects; 234 tinnitus, 101 controls) were projected onto a fixed seven-map microstate template. Pooled across datasets, 2/56 microstate statistics differed consistently, and after adjustment for pure-tone average (PTA) none remained significant after FDR correction. Tinnitus subjects had a larger fraction of fast-decaying Koopman modes in all three datasets, and this difference survived PTA adjustment (pooled r=0.26, p=0.002). Microstate differences in tinnitus are substantially explained by hearing level; operator-level dynamics of the same signal retain a hearing-adjusted difference that generalizes across sites.

items.title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
items.summary: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

items.title: A unified framework for net effects in signed social and ecological networks
items.summary: With improvements in data resolution and quality, researchers can now represent complex systems as signed, weighted, and directed networks. In this article, we introduce a framework for measuring net and indirect effects without simplifying these information-rich networks. It captures both direct and indirect interactions, the effect of the whole network on a node, and conversely, the effect of a node on the entire network, while accommodating the complexity of signed, weighted, and directed links. Our taxonomy unifies and extends existing approaches and measures from network science, computational social science, and ecological networks. We demonstrate its value in ecological systems, where net and indirect effects are critical yet difficult to quantify. Using generalized Lotka-Volterra dynamics, we find a strong correlation between negative net effects and species extinction. We further apply the framework to a real-world social network, where it identifies informative rankings that illuminate influence propagation and power dynamics.

items.title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation modulates auditory-evoked responses and conflict adaptation in humans
items.summary: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) engages ascending neuromodulatory systems, and animal studies have motivated the hypothesis that it shifts sensory cortical processing toward feedforward (FF) relative to feedback (FB) transmission. Whether transcutaneous auricular VNS (taVNS) produces a corresponding pattern in humans remains unclear. In a single-blind, sham-controlled crossover study, 11 healthy adults received 120 min of taVNS (25 Hz, left tragus) and sham stimulation (left earlobe) in separate sessions. Click-evoked EEG was recorded before, twice during, and immediately after stimulation. Sensory discrimination thresholds and conflict adaptation in a Simon task were assessed before and during stimulation. Relative to Sham, taVNS attenuated the decline in the early P0 response across the session and enhanced the Pa-Nb response early during stimulation. The later P2 response did not show the increase observed under Sham. After stimulation, taVNS reduced click-locked theta (5-8 Hz) inter-trial phase coherence relative to Sham, with no significant between-condition difference in the change in theta power. Conflict adaptation increased under taVNS, whereas sensory thresholds and the overall Simon effect did not differ significantly between conditions. In exploratory analysis, greater decreases in theta phase coherence were associated with greater increases in conflict adaptation. These findings indicate that taVNS modulates auditory responses across processing stages and conflict-related behavior. The pattern is compatible with altered FF/FB weighting, but the direction of information flow and the underlying neuromodulatory mechanisms were not measured directly.

items.title: From antidepressants to psychedelics: revisiting the pharmacology of so-called serotoninergic treatments
items.summary: Recent years have seen a resurgence of interest in serotoninergic psychedelics as potential treatment for diverse psychiatric disorders. Here, we will delve into the molecular mechanisms of drugs used to treat depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), with implications on the mechanism of action of so-called ''serotoninergic'' psychedelics as well as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). In particular, we argue that the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of SSRIs suggest that the inhibition of the serotonin transporter (SERT) alone does not provide a comprehensive account of their clinical effects. On the contrary, the SSRI posology required to treat depression and OCD is consistent with their major molecular target(s) displaying an SSRI affinity much lower than SERT. Such is the case for the tyrosine receptor kinase B (TrkB), recently described as a putative target for drugs with antidepressant effects. TrkB might thus provide a unifying framework for understanding the therapeutic effects of antidepressant drugs. We finally discuss the pharmacological implications of this hypothesis on the therapeutical potential of psychedelics.

items.title: Adventures in Multi-Omics I: Combining heterogeneous data sets via relationships matrices
items.summary: In this article, we propose a covariance based method for combining partial data sets in the genotype to phenotype spectrum. In particular, an expectation-maximization algorithm that can be used to combine partially overlapping relationship/covariance matrices is introduced. Combining data this way, based on relationship matrices, can be contrasted with a feature imputation based approach. We used several public genomic data sets to explore the accuracy of combining genomic relationship matrices. We have also used the heterogeneous genotype/phenotype data sets in the https://triticeaetoolbox.org/ to illustrate how this new method can be used in genomic prediction, phenomics, and graphical modeling.

items.title: multiCAsp: Spatially Informed Canonical Association Analysis of Multi-Omic Data
items.summary: Simultaneous profiling of multiple molecular layers at spatially resolved locations creates opportunities to identify shared cross-modal biological variation in its tissue context. We present multiCAsp (multi-omic Canonical Association informed by spatial graph), a probabilistic latent-factor model for integrating $M \geq 2$ spatially resolved omic modalities. It incorporates spatial dependence through a graph-Laplacian prior on shared latent factors and uses an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate factor scores and modality-specific feature loadings. Because the prior is defined on a neighborhood graph rather than on Euclidean distances, it accommodates irregular tissue geometries and extends naturally to multiple tissue sections. Simulations show that multiCAsp consistently achieves higher mean latent subspace and loading recovery than alternative methods across varying sample sizes, feature dimensions, and noise levels, with the largest gains under high noise. Compared with an existing Gaussian process-based spatial factor model, it is also less sensitive to how the spatial coordinates are represented, produces spatially smoother factors, and has lower computational cost. Applied to metabolomic-proteomic data from macaque cortex and gene-protein data from human renal carcinoma, multiCAsp recovers spatially coherent multi-omic factors with interpretable biological signatures. In the macaque data, transferred factors retain broad spatial patterns across animals and support cross-modal prediction of protein abundances from metabolomic measurements.

items.title: What makes vertical federated learning work with thirteen samples? A controlled benchmark on coral thermal-stress multi-omics
items.summary: Vertical federated learning (VFL) lets laboratories that hold different omics layers of the same samples train a joint model without sharing raw data, but it is usually developed for datasets with thousands of samples. We benchmarked VFL on a Montipora capitata thermal-stress dataset with 13 samples and 90,579 features across transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and microbiome data. The benchmark crosses two VFL backbones (a split-network model implemented in NVIDIA FLARE, and LASER-VFL) with three per-silo feature-selection strategies (gradient saliency, random, univariate t-test) and two allocations of a 1,300-feature budget, and adds a centralised elastic-net reference. All models were trained for the same number of steps and evaluated by repeated stratified 3-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation, with separate estimates of seed and data-split variability and end-to-end label-permutation tests. Plain VFL on all features classified heat stress well above chance (3-fold AUROC 0.869, 95% CI 0.838-0.895; permutation p = 0.020). Gradient-saliency selection with hand-set omics priors (0.904) could not be distinguished from plain VFL, from equal budgets or from random subsets of the same size (corrected p >= 0.56), and its selected features were no more consistent across seeds than random ones. LASER-VFL failed on all features at a learning rate of 1e-3 but matched the other methods at 1e-4. This version corrects versions 1-3 of this preprint, which reported that standard VFL performed at chance and that domain priors stabilised training; we show that those results arose because every model selected its checkpoint on a single-sample validation set, which evaluated the baseline after one optimiser step. With very few samples, evaluation choices outweighed every method choice we tested, and we give recommendations for evaluating federated models in this regime.

items.title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
items.summary: Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.

items.title: CellChain: Benchmarking Cross-Scale Evidence Use for Perturbation Reasoning
items.summary: Recent advances in foundation models and large-scale cellular perturbation datasets have driven growing interest in using LLMs to predict and reason about cellular responses. Biological reasoning in this setting involves relating molecular mechanisms, cellular responses, and functional outcomes across scales. Evaluating foundation models therefore requires assessing not only whether their predictions are correct, but also how those predictions depend on the biological evidence provided. We introduce CellChain, an experimentally grounded benchmark comprising 590 biological cases and 2,360 matched evidence-condition instances across gene-dependency prediction, cytokine-axis identification, and drug-sensitivity ranking. CellChain links perturbation experiments and external biological resources through a provenance-aware evidence graph spanning molecular, pathway, transcriptional, and phenotypic information. Task-specific conditions vary evidence coverage, composition, or assignment while preserving questions, candidate answers, reference targets, and scoring rules. Across 18 foundation models, the highest accuracies under prespecified target-evidence conditions are 57.5%, 75.5%, and 70.8%, respectively, and broader evidence coverage does not consistently improve accuracy. On the drug-sensitivity benchmark cohort, matched reference histories outperform swapped histories by an average of 13.0 percentage points in cluster-weighted accuracy. Decision-transition analysis separates corrections, newly introduced errors, and wrong-answer switches, revealing substantial answer changes hidden by small net accuracy differences. CellChain provides controlled comparisons for attributing changes in model predictions to prespecified expansions of biological context, including changes in evidence coverage, composition, and biological assignment.

items.title: High-Fidelity 3D Simulator for Synthetic fNIRS Data Generation
items.summary: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides a noninvasive window into brain activity by measuring task-related changes in oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin in the cortex. However, analyzing fNIRS data is challenging because of motion artifacts, physiological noise, and other confounding factors. This challenge is further compounded by the limited availability of annotated datasets, which hinders the development and validation of new analysis pipelines, particularly given the growing use of AI methods. Recognizing these challenges, we introduce a 3D fNIRS simulator that uses mesh-based Monte Carlo simulations to generate physiologically informed, full-head synthetic recordings with controllable spatiotemporal characteristics. Our simulator combines anatomically informed sensitivity profiles with parameterized models of hemodynamic responses, systemic physiology, and measurement artifacts. As a result, users can generate large labeled datasets with known cortical ground truth for developing and evaluating denoising algorithms, data augmentation strategies, mechanistic models, and in silico experiments. We validate key spatiotemporal and physiological properties of the simulator against experimental fNIRS data from open-source finger-tapping, pain-assessment, and surgical-skill datasets.

items.title: iEEG Can Help EEG: Improving Clinical Scalp EEG Analysis through Intracranial Priors
items.summary: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone of clinical brain monitoring, making the quality of its signal fundamental to downstream tasks and models. However, that signal is heavily contaminated by non-neural interference and blurred by volume conduction. Existing methods operate almost exclusively within the scalp modality, so they inherit the contamination they would need to overcome. In practice, intracranial EEG (iEEG) observes the neural activity with far higher fidelity, yet it is invasive and therefore scarce, and the two modalities are rarely recorded as pairs at scale, share no common channel space, and offer no clean ground truth to directly supervise a mapping. Motivated by the neuronal synchronization mechanism shared by the two modalities, we propose a reprogramming approach that fits a signal-to-signal model on iEEG alone and freezes it as a cross-modal prior. We introduce ReBrain, a framework to transfer an iEEG-learned prior to scalp EEG, which re-expresses any scalp signal through that prior and can be inserted upstream of any downstream model with no pairing or fine-tuning. ReBrain consistently improves host models across recordings from multiple hospitals and across architecture families, and our analysis traces this gain to genuine neural structure carried by iEEG rather than to the architecture itself. This work provides evidence that a scarce clean modality can serve as a transferable prior for an abundant noisy one, offering a general recipe for cross-modal transfer among biosignals. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xianglong-Bao/ReBrain.

items.title: HoloGene: Learning to Lift Sliced Spatial Transcriptomics to Holistic 3D Gene Fields
items.summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression measurements, but most 3D ST datasets are acquired as independently processed 2D sections. Computational approaches span slice registration and integration, explicit or generative interpolation, and coordinate-field modeling. Within the last family, implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a continuous, coordinate-queryable parameterization, but standard isotropic coordinate encodings do not explicitly reflect that serial-section measurements are dense in-plane and sparse along the axial direction. We present HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional INR framework for estimating continuous 3D gene-expression fields from pre-registered ST sections. Its central contribution is an acquisition-aware factorization that couples dense in-plane synthesis with sparse axial evolution using established GAE, FiLM, pseudo-label supervision, and CORAL components. HoloGene compresses high-dimensional expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, uses pseudo-label-derived signature conditioning to provide coarse intra-section context, and applies depth-dependent FiLM modulation to model axial variation. A signature-stratified correlation-alignment regularizer encourages cross-slice covariance alignment in latent features. Using held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene improves reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics compared with general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines. These results support anisotropic conditional modeling as a practical strategy for estimating 3D expression fields from discontinuous ST sections. Code is available at https://github.com/Szym29/HoloGene.

items.title: Beyond AUC: Do Mammography Risk Models Predict When Cancer Occurs?
items.summary: Longitudinal deep learning models for mammography-based breast cancer risk prediction output either per-year cumulative risks or a discrete distribution over the year of diagnosis, from which cumulative risks F1,...,F5 are derived. These models are evaluated almost exclusively with year-wise AUCs and the concordance index. We show that these metrics are largely insensitive to when cancer occurs: they can be high even for a model that carries no information about the year of diagnosis. We re-evaluate two recent longitudinal models (OA-BreaCR, LMV-Net) on CSAW-CC with a 5-year horizon using timing metrics computed on cancer cases only. Despite C-indices up to 0.75, neither orders cancer cases by time to diagnosis significantly better than chance (c_time 0.51 and 0.55, both 95% CIs covering 0.5). Weighted absolute timing error favours a constant "year 3" prediction over both models, so we use c_time as the primary timing metric. For Mirai's additive-hazard head, also used by LMV-Net, we analyse how per-year increments passed through a ReLU can collapse under severe class imbalance. We also propose a breast-level, two-stage model that separates whether from when. It matches LMV-Net in discrimination (C-index 0.745 vs. 0.746) but orders cancer cases better (c_time 0.58 vs. 0.51, paired 95% CI of the difference 0.01-0.13), on par with Mirai's published weights (0.57).

items.title: Feedback-induced mechanical bistability and perpendicular-domain formation in active elastic tissues
items.summary: Contractile fibers in muscle tissues are highly aligned over the scale of many cells. Muscle layers surrounding organs with an inner lumen are often arranged in orthogonal directions. Here, we study a minimal mechanism of how structural order and its patterning into orthogonally aligned domains can emerge from mechanical feedback alone. The central idea is that contractile fibers align in the direction of the local active and elastic stresses, a feedback motivated by the maturation of muscle fibers under tension. We thus model muscle tissue as an active nematic solid with stress feedback: an elastic medium with embedded contractile fibers that are reinforced along the directions of the local tissue stresses. We find that the feedback from the contractile fiber stress is self-amplifying and drives spontaneous fiber alignment. Feedback from the elastic stress couples the alignment to the mechanical boundary conditions and tissue geometry. Depending on the mechanical boundary conditions, the elastic-stress feedback stabilizes two orthogonally aligned tissue states, resulting in a structurally and mechanically bistable tissue that shows a hysteretic stress-strain response. In spatially extended tissues, this bistability gives rise to orthogonally aligned domains separated by domain walls. Our results show that stress feedback can pattern structural order by coupling spontaneous alignment to the tissue geometry. Our mechanism thus provides a purely mechanical route to orthogonal fiber patterning in muscle tissues.

items.title: Stochastic partial differential equation model for environmental DNA dynamics in river environments
items.summary: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has emerged as a novel tool for quantifying the seasonal abundance of aquatic species in water bodies; however, its mathematical modeling is still at a germinating stage because of its mechanistic uncertainties. We propose a first-step mathematical and computational framework for the eDNA dynamics of migratory fish based on a novel stochastic partial differential equation model with a delayed source input. The model governs spatiotemporal eDNA concentration in rivers where the source comes from a stochastic differential equation for the migration dynamics of the fish. The affine nature of the model facilitates its theoretical analysis, including the guarantee of well-posedness and the closed-form derivation of the Laplace functional despite the proportionality coefficient of the multiplicative noise term being non-Lipschitz. We also propose a discretization scheme for the model that theoretically generates nonnegative numerical solutions. We finally apply the proposed model to eDNA concentration data sampled from midstream reaches of a river system and perform sensitivity analysis.

items.title: Scaling large language model-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication with human-in-the-loop evidence-calibrated selection
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the ability to scale clinical adjudication tasks traditionally dependent on exhaustive manual review. Line-of-therapy (LoT) adjudication, a major bottleneck in oncology cohort construction, is a prime example. Line boundaries must be inferred from longitudinal treatment histories according to nuanced, study-specific definitions, at every regimen transition for every patient. LLMs can apply this adjudication at scale, but their reliability varies across patients. Treatment histories differ in complexity, and ambiguous or atypical patterns depend on expert clinical judgment. Reliable automation thus requires verified support for model assignments and the ability to identify cases that warrant manual review. Here, we present evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework for scaling LLM-assisted LoT adjudication. ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and returns completed adjudications to the model as precedent. As the evidence base grows, ECS continuously calibrates confidence to estimate residual error, thus enabling more efficient use of clinician time. In simulations on 136 clinician adjudicated patients with multiple myeloma, ECS achieved a residual error of 5% after review of 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% when review was directed by LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling. These results support a scalable approach to study-specific LoT adjudication, using clinician evidence to inform automated predictions, minimize error, and reduce review burden.

items.title: Atheism and Cross-Country National Cognitive Skills: Evidence from a Beta Regression Analysis
items.summary: This study performs a beta regression analysis to investigate how country-level cognitive skills---measured using harmonized large-scale international educational assessments and expressed on an IQ-type scale---are associated with the prevalence of atheism in 131 countries. We find that this association is nonlinear: at low levels of cognitive skills, increases are associated with lower expected levels of atheism, whereas beyond a threshold, they are associated with higher expected atheism rates. This turning point is estimated to occur at approximately 65 on the IQ-type scale. The strength and location of the relationship vary across regions. We estimate elasticities of expected atheism rates with respect to cognitive skills for all countries in the sample and introduce the concept of the atheism gap to identify countries where observed prevalence is substantially higher or lower than predicted by their conditioning variables.

items.title: Robust Twoblock Simultaneous Dimension Reduction and Multivariate Regression
items.summary: This paper introduces robust twoblock (RTB) simultaneous dimension reduction, which is the first statistically robust method to perform simultaneous dimension reduction in two blocks of variables that allows to tune the number of components in each block individually. The paper proposes both a dense and a sparse version of the new method. Sparse RTB is the first robust estimator of this kind that allows to tune both the number of components and the degree of sparsity (i.e.\ the number of variables retained) for each block individually. RTB thereby allows to optimally extract and summarize the relevant portion of information in each block of data, also in the presence of outliers. As a corollary, the estimators can be recombined into a single estimate of regression coefficients for multivariate regression that is operable when the number of variables exceeds the number of cases in each block. An extensive simulation study illustrates that the new methods are resistant to different types of outliers, while maintaining estimation efficiency across a range of dimensionality settings. These findings both hold true for the dense and the sparse method. The methods' performance is further illustrated on two example data sets and a straightforward algorithm is presented and made accessible in an open source repository.

items.title: Modeling time series of high-resolution spectra using the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition with application to radial velocity exoplanet searches
items.summary: We describe a framework for building low-rank separable expansions to model spectroscopic data from systems with time-varying spectra, in settings where the spectral dimension is finely sampled (in wavelength), but the temporal dimension is sparsely and possibly irregulary sampled. The motivating application is detection and characterization of small exoplanets, e.g., Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars. Such planets cannot be seen directly, but can be detected via the minute Doppler shifts of the host star spectrum due to the star's motion as the planet and star revolve around their mutual center of mass. Current instruments are reaching the precision necessary to detect the ~10 cm/s motions corresponding to an exo-Earth. But the small Doppler shifts from such low-amplitude orbital motion can be masked or mimicked by the effects of stellar activity on the surface of the host star. e.g., starspots (dark regions), faculae (bright filaments), etc. One technique astronomers have used to try to model the stellar activity component of the signal is PCA, applied to an ensemble of spectra collected over time. But PCA neglects the continuous function nature of a spectrum at a given time, and the continuous evolution of spectra over time. We address model building from a function approximation perspective, via the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition (HSD). This provides a PCA-like low-rank decomposition of a dynamic spectrum, but it explicitly accounts for time dependence, both estimating temporal basis functions, and accounting for irregular temporal sampling when estimating spectral basis functions. We show that HSD improves the fidelity of a fixed-order model of the dynamic spectrum of a Sun-like star with a starspot, with mean squared error for spectral basis functions many times smaller than achieved via PCA when spectra are randomly sampled sparsely and irregularly in time.

items.title: Who Fills the Gap? Role Similarity and Teammates' Minutes When NBA Players Are Ruled Out
items.summary: When a core player is ruled out before an NBA game, do teammates whose statistical role resembles that of the removed set (every rotation player ruled out, about three per case) play more? Using injury reports stamped at least six hours before tip-off and rosters reconstructed after the season, we study 2,441 team-games from 2023-24 to 2025-26 in which a core player was ruled out for a medical reason. Among teammates in the same game, one within-case standard deviation more similarity in role profile (three-point attempts, assists and rebounds per minute) goes with about 0.63 more minutes, holding reference minutes and headroom fixed (p < 0.0001); this compares teammates within a game, not the minutes gained because of the absence. The pattern holds in two earlier seasons and in exploratory within-player and without-and-with comparisons. Whether similarity adds to listed position is not settled. The association is small and yielded no statistically detectable reduction in the error of the retrospective minute forecasts we tested. Role coverage, how much of the missing minutes and roles the remaining rotation could restore, showed no consistent incremental association with team role output or the final margin.

items.title: Distribution-Free Changepoint Inference for Rainfall Patterns
items.summary: Long records of rainfall contain critical information about the temporal organization of precipitation within a year, including wet and dry spells. Detecting when this temporal pattern changes is central to climate-impact assessment and environmental monitoring.A common data structure features observations from m locations over T years. For location i and year t, the record is a vector of daily measurements $X_{i,t} = (X_{i,t,1}, ..., X_{i,t,D})^\top$, with D = 365. The goal is to identify an unknown year $t_0$ when the temporal rainfall pattern changes across the region. Because changes in the intra-annual pattern affect the frequency-domain behavior of the daily sequence, we represent each yearly curve through a spectral feature capturing the strength of temporal oscillation at a fixed frequency.Classical changepoint methods often rely on parametric likelihoods or Gaussian approximations, which are hard to justify for skewed and heavy-tailed rainfall data. Furthermore, many procedures only return a point estimate. A confidence set for the change year is crucial in environmental applications to quantify temporal uncertainty and distinguish sharp transitions from weak evidence.This paper develops a distribution-free framework for detecting a synchronized structural change in yearly rainfall patterns across independently monitored locations. For each location-year pair, we compute a fixed-frequency nonparametric spectral density estimate. These features form a $T \times m$ data matrix. By exploiting the exchangeability of yearly spectral features before and after the true changepoint, alongside spatial independence, we construct finite-sample valid confidence sets for the unknown change year.

items.title: The Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model as a Statistical Model: Identification, Estimation, and Model Comparison
items.summary: The random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) distinguishes stable differences between people from lagged associations within individuals. We use a matrix representation to study its statistical properties for p variables measured across T waves. We derive a necessary and sufficient rank condition for global identification when transition matrices and innovation covariances vary by wave. Under time-invariant transitions, the condition specifies when three waves suffice. For complete Gaussian trajectories, matrix differentiation yields the profile likelihood score for each covariance and transition block. We also derive the population parameters of the conventional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) when an RI-CLPM with fixed parameters generates the data. Our formulas quantify how CLPM slopes for observed variables differ from RI-CLPM slopes for within-person deviations at each transition. When the RI-CLPM transition matrix is time-invariant, the comparison also covers CLPM slopes pooled across waves. The formulas recover earlier bivariate results and show when cross-lagged slopes can appear, cancel, reverse sign, or change their ordering across models.

items.title: Minimising sample size across analysis strategies in preclinical research: Reduced power or negligible benefit
items.summary: Preclinical animal studies often allow multiple valid statistical analysis strategies, which can result in different sample sizes required to achieve a target power. Because reducing animal use is an ethical, financial, and practical priority, researchers have a clear incentive to choose the strategy requiring the fewest animals. This may, however, favour an overly optimistic estimate of the sample size required, particularly when prior information is uncertain or biased. This study investigates how minimising sample size across analysis strategies affects statistical power and animal use. We conceptualise this practice as sample size hacking, describe its underlying mechanism, and evaluate its consequences using a simulation study based on a real preclinical cancer study. We varied effect sizes, the level of uncertainty in prior information, and the degree of follow-up bias to assess the resulting sample size reductions and achieved statistical power. Sample size minimisation across analysis strategies substantially reduced the achieved statistical power in several scenarios, particularly for moderate effect sizes and greater uncertainty in prior information. For larger effect sizes or in the presence of follow-up bias, the impact on power was less pronounced, but the resulting reduction in sample size was also smaller. Selecting an analysis strategy solely because it yields the smallest calculated sample size may in fact compromise statistical power, while offering only limited animal savings in other settings. These findings underscore the importance of justifying and pre-specifying the analysis strategy before sample size planning to limit potentially problematic analytical flexibility, reduce the risk of underpowered studies, and promote transparency in preclinical research.

items.title: Projection of multidimensional count data IRT models and their empirical indistinguishability
items.summary: Empirical test data is rarely unidimensional. If one dimension is of interest, projective item-response-theory (IRT) models can be used to work with a unidimensional model without neglecting the multidimensionality of the data. This work extends the projective IRT literature to count data IRT models from the Two-Parameter Conway-Maxwell-Poisson model framework. We build on the definition of empirical indistinguishability and analytically derive closed-form expressions for discrimination parameters and item intercepts after projection. The dispersion parameters of the projected Two- Parameter Conway-Maxwell-Poisson model are obtained with numerical approximations. The analytical calculations are not limited to the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson distribution. In addition, rotation methods are applied before projection. Results are illustrated and evaluated using empirical data from cognitive ability assessment items and in a simulation study. The projected model performed better in terms of RMSE, Spearman correlation between the true and estimated person parameters, and coverage of 95% confidence intervals based on the Fisher information than an approximation by a standard unidimensional model fitted to multidimensional data. No improvement in bias over the standard unidimensional model, nor improvement across all metrics over the multidimensional model, were observed.

items.title: Analytical Wald Power for Lagged Coefficients in the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model
items.summary: In a longitudinal study, the number of participants and the number of waves both affect how much power the study has to detect a lagged effect. The random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) is widely used to study within-person dynamics, but existing approaches to power analysis for this model typically rely on simulation or target likelihood-ratio tests. Starting from the likelihood score, we derive analytical Wald power for each lagged coefficient in the bivariate RI-CLPM. Across 30 designs, we compared our analytical results with power estimates from two R packages, powRICLPM for simulated Wald power and semPower for analytical likelihood-ratio power. The mean absolute difference was less than one percentage point in each comparison. By avoiding repeated simulation and model fitting, the analytical method saves time when evaluating power for a target path across many combinations of sample size (N) and number of waves (T).

items.title: Evaluating laser scanning data sources, canopy metrics, and predictor resolution for forest inventory
items.summary: Forest managers updating growing stock volume (GSV) estimates must decide whether existing LiDAR data calibrated with current inventory are sufficient or a new acquisition provides worthwhile improvements. We compared regional airborne laser scanning (ALS) acquired in 2023 with uncrewed aerial vehicle laser scanning (ULS) from 2026 in a mixed-species forest in north-eastern Germany. Both datasets were calibrated using the same 2026 personal laser scanning inventory within a change-of-support regression framework. We compared 3 m and 35 m grids, canopy height alone and with three structural metrics, and models with and without spatial random effects. Evaluation comprised 10-fold cross-validation (CV) on 118 undisturbed plots (no tree removal), prediction on 33 disturbed plots (detected removal) excluded from calibration, and CV across all 151 plots. In undisturbed CV, the lowest root mean squared prediction errors (RMSPEs) were 74.1 m3 ha-1 for ULS and 81.5 m3 ha-1 for ALS, a 9.1% reduction for ULS. Both used spatial effects and 3 m predictors, with structural metrics for ULS and canopy height only for ALS. At 3 m, canopy-height-only models performed similarly across sources, whereas adding structural metrics improved ULS predictions. Finer grids improved both sources, and spatial effects gave only small gains. On the disturbed holdout, 3 m ULS models had little bias, whereas ALS overpredicted volume, consistent with predictors representing pre-removal conditions. Canopy-height-only ULS outperformed the four-predictor models on these plots. Across all 151 plots, the 3 m four-predictor ULS models achieved an RMSPE of 70.5 m3 ha-1 versus 81.5 m3 ha-1 for the best ALS model, a 13.5% reduction. Existing ALS therefore retained substantial predictive value on undisturbed plots, while ULS provided additional information and supported estimation across both disturbance classes.

items.title: A Family of Quantile Functions Useful in Clinical Studies
items.summary: Survival comparisons usually rest on means, medians or hazard ratios. These summaries say little about patients who live beyond a given time, and two treatments with similar medians can differ in this upper tail. We therefore study the quantile-based effectiveness persistence function defined as the ratio between the tail mean and the quantile function. Motivated by upper-tail quantile-domain summaries, we derive statistical properties of this measure and consider a rational (Möbius) specification of the quantile-based effectiveness persistence function. Under natural boundary conditions, this specification reduces to a canonical form, in which remaining life relative to elapsed time is proportional to the survival odds. The resulting canonical family defines a two-parameter class of non-negative distributions through its quantile function. Various properties, including descriptive measures, L-moments, and quantile-based reliability concepts, are derived for this class. For two treatment arms, the family gives a contrast that is constant over quantile levels without assuming proportional hazards. Estimation of the model parameters using maximum likelihood is also developed. The proposed family is illustrated using two real survival datasets.

items.title: The Last Expectation: Sampling Measurement Outcomes in Value of Information Analysis
items.summary: In decision-making under uncertainty, additional information can improve decisions but is often costly to acquire. The Value of Information (VoI) quantifies the expected benefit of different information-gathering strategies. The main computational burden in VoI analysis arises from evaluating the expected utility of a strategy over possible outcomes. As each outcome entails solving a computationally expensive optimization problem under uncertainty to determine the optimal decision, efficient estimation of this expectation is crucial. This work focuses on sampling-based estimation and investigates three classical variance-reduction techniques, namely control variates, stratified sampling, and importance sampling, as well as combinations thereof. In particular, we establish a connection between two common VoI formulations through a control variate framework and show how this relationship can be exploited to obtain more efficient VoI estimators. The methodology is assessed using three test cases. The first is an analytical example with a known reference solution, the second involves a fatigue reliability and the third a slope stability application. Our results demonstrate that the relative performance of the sampling methods depends strongly on the problem characteristics. However, suitable combinations of variance-reduction techniques consistently improve efficiency and provide stable VoI estimates across a range of scenarios.

items.title: Bayesian Computation of Copula-based Multivariate Models with an Application to Doping Detection
items.summary: The Athlete Biological Passport (ABP) monitors athletes for doping by comparing their biomarker readings against personalized reference ranges. These are estimated via the Bayesian ADAPTIVE model, which analyzes biomarkers separately and ignores their dependence. Building on a recently proposed copula-based multivariate extension of ADAPTIVE, this paper focuses on its computational aspects, introducing a fully joint MCMC algorithm and comparing it with a two-step Bayesian IFM estimator. Simulations show the two procedures perform comparably under a correctly specified copula, but exhibit a genuine trade-off under misspecification: the Bayesian IFM protects marginal inference, while the joint MCMC yields better-calibrated dependence estimates and is markedly faster. The two approaches are tested on a dataset containing ABP profiles of elite athletes, provided by NADO Italia, and collected as part of the project "Enhancing the methodological framework for doping detection: from univariate to multivariate testing analysis on Athlete Biological Passport profiles". Both approaches achieve consistent classification performance, providing anti-doping organizations with two concrete inferential routes for adopting a multivariate ADAPTIVE model, along with guidance on the trade-offs between them.

items.title: Guiding Multi-Objective Genetic Programming with Description Length Improves Symbolic Regression Solutions
items.summary: Symbolic regression with genetic programming (GPSR) may suffer from overfitting and structural bloat, especially when noise is present. In this paper we evaluate description length (DL) and fractional Bayes factor (FBF) criteria as principled, data-efficient alternatives to heuristics for selecting compact expressions that generalise well. We implement DL using a Fisher-information-based parameter encoding and compare it to the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) across multiple datasets, including noisy synthetic benchmarks and real-world regression problems. We study three search/selection strategies: (i) multi-objective search for accuracy and program length followed by DL/FBF selection; (ii) multi-objective search using DL directly as an objective; and (iii) single-objective optimisation with DL/FBF as the fitness. Across datasets, we find that DL/FBF post-selection improves test performance compared to AIC/BIC baseline and that BIC in combination with the same function complexity penalty from DL/FBF produces similar results. In contrast, using DL/FBF directly as a fitness function in single-objective GPSR frequently induces premature convergence to overly simple models. We conclude with practical guidance for using DL/FBF as robust model-selection tools in genetic programming workflows.

items.title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
items.summary: On the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the 1D flat torus, we exhibit a distribution where a recent extension of Riemannian flow matching is globally optimized by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data distribution. We trace this failure mode to a property we call compatibility; a likelihood-based flow matching objective is compatible if its population minimizer recovers the marginal velocity field induced by the data and coupling. We derive a general condition for compatibility, apply it to existing methods, and bound the worst-case error by a residual term that vanishes under compatibility. On compact manifolds, we show that existing compatible objectives put density on infeasible velocities. To tackle both issues, we propose an exponential family over endpoints with the conditional velocity as sufficient statistic, which is both compatible and supported only on feasible velocities. In practice, and with low overhead, this reduces to a reweighting of the flow matching loss. On spaces of constant curvature, this treats errors in flow speed and direction differently. Compared to prior art, our method finds the correct velocities on the test case, outperforms in general on high-dimensional product tori, and, for two of four standard geospatial benchmarks on the sphere, achieves substantial NLL improvements. When evaluated on a large dataset of human poses, our method surpasses prior work according to sample-based metrics.

items.title: BADGERS: Bayesian Adaptive Graph-Guided Errors-in-Variables Regression Solution for Structured High-Dimensional Data
items.summary: Knowledge-guided learning methods that incorporate biological graph information into the analysis of structured high-dimensional data, such as genomic data, can improve variable selection and prediction accuracy while yielding more interpretable results. However, these methods typically assume that covariates are measured without error. This assumption is often violated in omics studies involving replicated measurements. To address this gap, we develop the Bayesian Adaptive Graph-guided Errors-in-variables Regression Solution (BADGERS), a Bayesian framework that jointly accounts for covariate measurement error and incorporates graph information while accommodating varying numbers of replicates across covariates. BADGERS treats the true covariates as latent variables and integrates three key components: a Gaussian errors-in-variables model using replicated measurements to inform the latent true covariates, a Bayesian adaptive graphical lasso with a graph-informed prior to model their dependence structure, and a regression model with an adaptive structured shrinkage prior to leverage graph information and facilitate variable selection. We develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for posterior sampling. We demonstrate the advantages of BADGERS over existing methods through simulation studies and analyses of gene expression datasets for Alzheimer's disease and multiple myeloma.

items.title: Guarded Readmission Weighting for Robust Single-Index Frechet Regression
items.summary: Single-index Frechet regression reduces the predictor dimension for metric-space responses such as distributions, networks or curves, but its estimators are sensitive to outliers. We propose guarded readmission weighting (GRW), a one-step computation of case weights from the predictors and the response distances, usable with any weighted estimator. GRW starts from a high-breakdown fit to a multidimensional scaling surrogate, readmits cases by an add-one metric Cook's distance, downweights remote predictors and keeps a response isolation factor in the final weights. If fewer than $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ of the $n$ cases are replaced, objects far from the uncontaminated responses receive weight zero; under elliptical predictors, weights depending on the predictors only through the index and the Mahalanobis distance keep the population weighted directions in the index subspace. In simulations, three GRW-weighted estimators keep the mean projection distance to the true direction below about 0.5 under up to 30% scattered and 20% clustered bad leverage points, whereas deletion and $α$-distance covariance become much less accurate as contamination grows; $α$-distance covariance is more accurate in most clean, shape-outlier and good-leverage settings. In two applications, under planted contamination, the weighted surrogate-assisted and least squares directions move less than those of methods without GRW.

items.title: Pseudo-IPD Reconstruction from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves under Unidentified Within-Interval Censoring
items.summary: Reconstruction of pseudo-individual patient data (pseudo-IPD) from published Kaplan-Meier curves and number-at-risk tables is widely used to support secondary survival analyses when individual-level data are unavailable. However, the reconstruction is generally not unique because the published information does not determine how censoring is distributed within each risk-table interval. We study the non-identifiability that remains after interval-level event and censoring totals have been reconstructed. Different within-interval censoring placements can yield similarly good Kaplan-Meier agreement but different risk-set and censoring patterns, with possible effects on subsequent analyses. We characterize this non-identifiability, introduce a systematic allocation scheme, and assess its impact on reconstructed pseudo-IPD and downstream analyses. Simulation studies were conducted to examine how within-interval censoring allocation affects pseudo-IPD reconstruction under different risk-table resolutions and censoring settings. The proposed approach was also illustrated using published data from CheckMate 067. Our analysis suggests that considering multiple reconstructions provides a practical way to assess the impact of this non-identifiability on downstream analyses.

items.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
items.summary: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

items.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks
items.summary: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) is pivotal for modeling gene regulatory networks in cancer pathogenesis, yet single-study genomic data is often limited for accurate DAG reconstruction. Although multi-source datasets provide augmented sample sizes, substantial heterogeneity persists across real-world cohorts. It remains an open question how to pool the heterogeneous data with only local similarity together for better DAG structure reconstruction in the target study. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of structural similarity measures for DAGs and then present a transfer DAG learning framework by effectively leveraging information from auxiliary DAGs with node-level local similarities. Our theoretical analysis shows substantial improvement in terms of DAG reconstruction in the target study, which is in sharp contrast to most existing transfer learning methods requiring global similarity. The advantage of the proposed transfer DAG learning is also supported by extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic data and multi-source cancer genomics data.

items.title: Change Point Detection with Generative Models
items.summary: Change point detection (CPD) methods aim to identify abrupt changes in the properties of time series, which is a key problem in numerous fields. A major class of CPD approaches relies on computing a CPD score, which is either a discrepancy or divergence between two subsequent samples, called windows. A fundamental limitation of window-based CPD is the 'sample size bottleneck.' To ensure temporal precision, windows must be small; however, small samples provide insufficient statistical evidence for the classifiers and deep-learning models currently used to compute CPD scores. This leads to high variance in the scores and frequent mispredictions. Our study tackles this issue by exploring generative models for window augmentation, effectively expanding available data to improve CPD quality. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances CPD. Specifically, we show that this approach allows simple classifiers to outperform complex deep-learning baselines by stabilizing the CPD score distribution.

items.title: Critique of "Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses ..." by John O'Quigley
items.summary: The paper "Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses suspected of inflicting deliberate harm on patients" by Prof. John O'Quigley explores an interesting hypothesis concerning statistical information hidden in the part of the infamous Lucy Letby roster chart pertaining to the 37 other nurses. Unfortunately, we have to point out some serious errors in his statistical analyses. The data actually contains information which strongly disproves his main modelling assumption. We do, however, strongly agree with him that from a forensic statistical point of view, the roster chart is fake evidence which should not have been shown to jurors.

items.title: Permutation tests for Poisson network regression: Double semi-partialling, studentized statistics and actor effects
items.summary: The multiple regression quadratic assignment procedure (MRQAP) is a standard framework for inference on dyadic network data, and its properties are well established for the linear model. Network outcomes are often counts, modelled by Poisson regression with a log link. We prove that the invariance property of the Frisch--Waugh--Lovell theorem, the only part that double semi-partialling (DSP) requires, survives the nonlinear link. The DSP focal coefficient and its model-based, HC3 and dyadic cluster-robust standard errors coincide with those of the fit on the raw covariates. The choice between relabelling the raw focal array ($X$-permutation) and relabelling its DSP residual acts only on the reference distribution. The test holds its level when the relabelled designs reproduce the dependence that the statistic retains, and DSP reproduces the autocorrelation of the partialled focal covariate. When the raw focal array and its residual share their autocorrelation, the relabelling test holds the nominal level for all three statistics, at covariate correlations up to $0.9$ and in networks of $20$ to $100$ actors. A normal reference rejects a true null at rates up to $0.96$. With sender and receiver effects modelled, every statistic rejects a true null at $0.035$ to $0.070$ in all conditions, and power against a focal effect of $0.10$ rises from at most $32\%$ to at least $99.9\%$. When the actor effects cannot be modelled, adding the sender and receiver means of the nuisance covariates keeps DSP at its level. We give recommendations and illustrate the method on the EIES message-count network.

items.title: Statistical Inference for Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
items.summary: Privacy preservation in machine learning, particularly through Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), is crucial for analyzing sensitive data. However, existing statistical inference methods for SGD predominantly focus on cyclic subsampling, while DP-SGD requires randomized subsampling. This paper first bridges this gap by establishing the asymptotic properties of SGD under the randomized rule and extending these results to DP-SGD. For DP-SGD, we show that the asymptotic variance decomposes into statistical, sampling, and privacy-induced components. We propose two methods for constructing valid confidence intervals: the plug-in method and the random scaling method. We also perform extensive numerical analysis showing that the proposed confidence intervals achieve nominal coverage rates while maintaining privacy.

items.title: Beyond Gentrification: quantifying the economic, social and cultural dimensions of neighbourhood change through housing markets and digital traces
items.summary: Neighbourhood change is a multidimensional process in which economic, demographic, social and cultural transformations do not necessarily coincide over space and time. However, data driven approaches typically collapse these into single indices or regression models, losing the nuances of individual components. This paper integrates housing market, demographic and social media data (SMD) to characterise different configurations of neighbourhood change in Leeds and Bradford, UK. Rates of change (2014-2019) were estimated over Lower Super Output Areas for house prices relative to the 250 nearest neighbouring areas, and for residential mobility, ethnic composition, unemployment and professional occupation. Approximately 1.6 million geo-tagged tweets, filtered for personal users using a large language model (LLM), were analysed using Structural Topic Models with socio-economic prevalence covariates, LLM based neighbourhood characterisation and text embeddings scored against gentrification and decline archetypes. These measures were used as inputs to a model-based cluster analysis, which identified six distinct neighbourhood types, and a spatially varying multinomial GAM was used to examine the effects of changes in the inputs on cluster membership. The results show repeated divergence between structural and discursive trajectories: rapid turnover that is invisible in local SMD discourse, heritage villages experiencing amenity and incomer pressure, a settled British-Pakistani community whose stability would be mis-characterised as stagnation or decline, and marginal areas accumulating strain with little on-line signal. This suggests that SMD derived measures can provide independent information on neighbourhood character rather than simply confirming structural indicators, although low SMD signals may reflect under-detection rather than an absence of change.

items.title: United in Diversity? Contextual Biases in LLM-Based Predictions of the 2024 European Parliament Elections
items.summary: "Silicon samples" based on large language models (LLMs) have been argued to serve as efficient alternatives to surveys of humans, assuming that their training data includes information on human attitudes and behavior. However, LLM-generated survey data might exhibit biases, for example due to a lack of diversity in training and alignment processes, which risk reinforcing existing biases in research and policymaking. In this study, we examine to what extent LLM-based predictions of individual public opinion exhibit context-dependent biases by predicting the results of the 2024 EU elections. Before the elections have taken place, we prompt three LLMs with individual-level background information of 26,000 eligible European voters to predict each person's voting behavior. We show that when compared to the actual results, LLM-based predictions of future voting behavior largely fail, their accuracy is unequally distributed across national and linguistic contexts, and they require detailed attitudinal information in the prompt. The findings emphasize the limited applicability of silicon samples to public opinion prediction. In investigating their contextual biases, this study contributes to the understanding and mitigation of inequalities in the development of LLMs and their applications in computational social science.

items.title: Gaussian Process Stochastic Frontiers with Two-Way Fixed Effects
items.summary: Parametric frontier restrictions and unobserved time heterogeneity can distort efficiency measurement in panel data. This paper develops a Bayesian stochastic frontier model with a Gaussian process prior and unrestricted individual and time effects that may be correlated with inputs. Conditional on inefficiency, orthogonal projection eliminates both sets of fixed effects, yielding a restricted likelihood that retains observation-specific inefficiency. Monte Carlo experiments show competitive performance under correct parametric specification and improved performance when benchmark models impose an incorrect frontier functional form or omit time effects. An application to Spanish dairy farms observed from 1999 to 2010 yields similar average technical efficiency across specifications, but a lower posterior mean of average returns to scale, with greater uncertainty, under the Gaussian process frontier. Models with year effects also yield more stable estimated efficiency profiles than the benchmark with a quadratic trend and time-input interactions. These findings show that conclusions about scale economies and efficiency dynamics depend on both frontier flexibility and the treatment of time heterogeneity.

items.title: Accelerated Proximal Gradient Methods for Multiobjective Optimization over Probability Measures via Hilbert-Space Lifting
items.summary: Many sampling and inference tasks require a single distribution that balances several targets. We formulate this task as multiobjective optimization of Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences over probability measures, in the Pareto sense. The particle method MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2025) uses explicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version A-MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2026) lacks discrete-time guarantees. We propose the multiobjective Wasserstein proximal gradient (MWPG), which uses implicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version, multiobjective Wasserstein accelerated proximal gradient (MWAPG), with rigorous discrete-time guarantees. Our key idea is a Hilbert-space lifting: each measure is represented as the pushforward of a fixed base measure by a map in a Hilbert space. The problem then becomes a constrained multiobjective composite problem over transport maps, to which accelerated proximal gradient methods apply. For convex and smooth potentials, we show that MWAPG decreases a Pareto merit function at the rate $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$; for $m$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth potentials, the rate is $\mathcal{O}\big((1-\sqrt{m/L})^k\big)$. We also give closed-form Gaussian updates and particle implementations based on input-convex neural networks, which require no score estimation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world dataset show that MWAPG needs far fewer iterations than MWPG and matches or outperforms A-MWGraD in Bayesian multi-task learning.

items.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks
items.summary: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.96 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.

items.title: A new method of Ecological Inference based on the Cressie--Read power divergence
items.summary: Ecological inference aims to estimate the bivariate association structure between a pair of variables from the row and column totals of a set of contingency tables. The paper introduces a new approach based on minimizing the Cressie--Read power divergence, applied to the estimation of vote transitions between two elections. It also outlines a Fisher scoring algorithm and derives the asymptotic distribution of the estimator.

items.title: Design-based causal inference for ROC curves
items.summary: In randomized experiments, causal inference traditionally focuses on the average treatment effect, yet comparing the treatment and control potential outcome distributions is often of interest. Under complete randomization, we adopt a design-based framework without imposing an outcome model to study the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, which measures the proportion of treated outcomes exceeding each upper quantile of the control distribution. We propose an estimator that depends only on pooled outcome ranks, establish its asymptotic normality, and construct conservative variance estimators and confidence intervals. We also develop covariate adjustment directly for the ROC estimator, preserving the target estimand while achieving an asymptotic variance no larger than that of the unadjusted estimator. We further construct simultaneous confidence bands over an interior range of quantile levels and extend pointwise inference to the extreme upper tail of the control distribution, with both extensions accommodating covariate adjustment. Simulation studies and an application to a large-scale online learning experiment illustrate the proposed methods.

items.title: Nonparametric predictive inference for interval-censored data: M-functions anchored to the self-consistent estimator
items.summary: Nonparametric predictive inference specifies the distribution of a future observation through M-functions, which are basic probability assignments on intervals. Here such a specification is proposed for data censored on the left, on the right or within intervals of arbitrary width. It is the union of two M-functions. The first rests on a post-data assumption under which each censored observation divides its predictive mass equally amongst the observations with regions inside its own, and it reproduces the right-censored theory exactly. The second combines the Turnbull estimator with one unconstrained unit of predictive mass. The resulting survival bounds contain the Turnbull estimator, lie inside the bounds from all completions of the data and need no enumeration. In simulated inspection schemes they were calibrated for fixed events and for the rank of a further observation, while the second member alone was not. Equal weights on all orderings allowed by the data give the first member whenever the regions are nested or disjoint. The method is compared with the Turnbull estimator on two interval-censored studies.

items.title: A Tensor Neural Network for Interpretable and Predictive Representations
items.summary: Tensor regression is challenged by the exponential dimensionality of tensor-valued covariates and their complex multi-mode dependence. Existing methods therefore often rely on simple models, such as linear tensor regression and tensor additive models, which are computationally tractable but impose restrictive structural assumptions and may limit predictive accuracy.
